docs.title: ET Wealth Edition 25 October 2026
docs.text:
The NBFC (non-banking financial company) sector is expected to report healthy earnings for the September 2026 quarter, supported by robust credit demand, steady loan growth and stable asset quality. However, the operating environment may get tougher in the second half of Financial Year (FY) 2026-27 as higher interest rates push up funding costs.
 The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) recent 25 basis point repo rate hike, along with its shift to a ‘calibrated tightening stance’, suggests more interest rate hikes may be on the way. Analysts expect another 50 basis points of rate hikes during the rest of the year.
Funding costs are a key variable for NBFCs because they depend heavily on bank borrowings, bonds, commercial papers and other market instruments to fund their loan books. As interest rates move up, borrowing becomes more expensive, pushing up both fresh funding and refinancing costs. 
Early signs of this are visible. “Incremental cost of funds for NBFCs continued to inch up in the second quarter of FY27, particularly for lenders with greater reliance on market borrowings, as bond yields remained elevated amid geopolitical uncertainty,” noted Motilal Oswal Financial Services in a recent earnings preview report. In simple terms, NBFCs that raise more money through bonds and commercial paper are paying more for every fresh rupee they borrow.
Higher borrowing costs could gradually squeeze net interest margins (NIMs), a key indicator of lending profitability. NIM measures the spread between what a lender earns on loans and investments and what it pays on borrowings. Ishank Gupta, Analyst, Banking and Financial Services, Choice Institutional Equities, expects sector-wide NIM compression of 10-20 basis points over the next two to three quarters. The impact, however, is unlikely to be uniform. Much will depend on an NBFC’s funding profile, liability structure and ability to pass on higher borrowing costs to customers.
 Live Events
For investors, the bigger question is not just how NBFCs perform in the September quarter, but how well they manage a potentially tougher operating environment. Their ability to contain funding-cost pressures while preserving growth and asset quality will be critical in the coming quarters.
 Sharp rebound 
 Growth remains healthy
Despite concerns around rising rates, the sector’s growth drivers remain intact. Over the past few years, NBFCs have benefited from strong credit demand, better asset quality, healthy capital positions and broader funding sources. Business updates from several major players for the September 2026 quarter suggest growth remains broad-based, with healthy disbursements across housing, vehicle finance, gold loans and unsecured lending.
The sector has also benefited from a surge in banking system liquidity following the RBI’s special dollar-rupee swap facility linked to FCNR(B) deposits. Banks mobilised $127.2 billion through these deposits, easing liquidity conditions and supporting funding availability for NBFCs.
Against this backdrop, growth expectations remain strong. A recent Nuvama report expects several large retail and diversified NBFCs to maintain loan growth of 20-25% in the near term, supported by healthy credit demand and stable asset quality.
 Banking on a rally 
 Pressures emerging
While liquidity remains comfortable, it does not completely offset the impact of a rising rate environment. According to Nuvama, funding costs are likely to edge up as surplus liquidity normalises, which could start weighing on margins from FY2027-28.
Analysts also point to the sharp increase in bank lending to NBFCs after the RBI’s February 2025 risk-weight reduction. JM Financial estimates that bank credit to NBFCs grew 27% in FY2025-26, compared with about 6% in the previous year.
This matters because bank loans are usually linked to benchmarks such as the repo rate or EBLR (external benchmark lending rate) and are repriced relatively quickly. As a result, higher policy rates could be transmitted faster to NBFC borrowing costs than in previous cycles.
Not all lenders are equally vulnerable. NBFCs with a larger share of floating-rate loans and relatively stable liabilities are generally better placed to navigate a rising rate environment. Floating-rate assets allow them to pass on higher rates to borrowers more quickly, while fixed-rate liabilities help delay the impact of rising funding costs.
Housing finance companies may be relatively better positioned because a large proportion of their loan books are linked to floating rates. In contrast, lenders with a higher share of fixed-rate assets could face greater pressure on margins.
“Vehicle financiers, MFIs (microfinance institutions) and diversified NBFCs carry a larger fixed-rate book on the asset side and are expected to witness relatively higher margin pressure,” says Meghna Luthra, Research Analyst, InCred Capital Wealth Portfolio Managers. Another area investors are watching closely is the IRDAI’s consultation paper on insurance distribution reforms. If implemented as proposed, the commission caps could reduce insurance distribution income for some NBFCs and weigh on profitability.
 Valuations are reasonable
NBFC stocks have faced pressure this year amid geopolitical uncertainties, inflation concerns and the proposed IRDAI reforms. On an equal-weighted basis, the 60 NBFCs in the BSE Financial Services Index have declined 4.5% so far in 2026, with 43 stocks (or 72%) generating negative returns. The analysis is based on 13 October 2026 closing values. Analysts believe the correction reflects broader macro concerns rather than any significant deterioration in operating fundamentals. They also point out that valuations have become more reasonable after the recent decline.

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

Reliance Power 's board of directors on Monday approved the issuance of up to 46.20 crore equity shares/warrants worth Rs 1,525 crore via preferential allotment mode.
 The board has set the issue price at Rs 33 per share.
The issue price of equity shares/warrants is at a discount of 13% over Monday's closing price of Rs 38.15 on the NSE. The announcement was made after market hours and Reliance Power shares on Monday ended with gains of Rs 1.81 or 4.98% over the previous closing price.
 Reliance Infrastructure Limited, the promoter of the company, will enhance its equity stake by over Rs 600 crore, a company filing said. The other investors in the preferential issue are Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited and Sanatan Financial Advisory Services Private Limited.
The proceeds from the preferential issue will be utilised to expand business operations directly and/or through investment in subsidiaries and joint ventures, debt reduction and for general corporate purposes, the filing said.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.
 WATCH LIVE TODAY: Press conference with #FOMC Chair Powell at 2:30 p.m. ET: https://t.co/1uJrua5qsH https://t.co/FJa6TbkDMt pic.twitter.com/87g5NJITsz 
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

docs.title: Stock recommendations for 19 October from MarketSmith India
docs.text:
Markets 
 Stock recommendations for 19 October from MarketSmith India
 MarketSmith India 5 min read 19 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 MarketSmith India reveals its top stock recommendations for today, 19 October. Get expert insights into the best-performing stocks to guide your investment decisions. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Stock market recap : Indian equities recovered from early profit booking on Friday. The Sensex rose about 700 points from its intraday low. The gains were driven by a fourth straight session of buying in IT stocks, cooling bond yields, easing crude oil prices, and a rupee that strengthened for a fifth consecutive day. 
 The IT index jumped nearly 4% after Tech Mahindra's Q2 net profit rose 32.7% year on year to ₹ 1,585.6 crore, along with a dividend and a bonus issue. Wipro's revenue also beat estimates. In addition, a global selloff in AI-linked stocks pushed investors toward Indian software exporters, and the sector headed for its biggest weekly gain in 18 years. 
 Two stock recommendations by MarketSmith India:
 Buy: Goodluck India Limited (current price: ₹ 595) 
 Why it is recommended: Strong demand from the infrastructure, renewable energy, railways, and defence sectors is driving growth in the company's value-added engineering and steel products business. Capacity expansions and an increasing contribution from high-margin specialized products are supporting revenue growth and margin improvement. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 27.45, 52-week high: ₹ 615.00, volume: ₹ 46.50 crore 
 Technical analysis: Consolidation base breakout 
 Risk factors: Volatility in steel and raw material prices can impact profitability and working capital requirements. Dependence on cyclical sectors, such as construction and infrastructure, may lead to demand fluctuations during economic slowdowns.
 Buy: ₹ 589–598 
 Target price: ₹ 675 in two to three days 
 Stop loss : ₹ 555 
 Buy: FSN E-Commerce Ventures Limited (current price: ₹ 344)
 Why it is recommended: Rising online penetration of beauty and personal care products, coupled with Nykaa's strong brand positioning and omnichannel presence, supports sustained growth. Expansion of private labels, premium beauty brands, and fashion offerings is improving customer engagement and profitability. 
 Key metrics : P/E: 356.26, 52-week high: ₹ 349.55, volume: ₹ 91.13 crore 
 Technical analysis: Bounce back from its 21-DMA 
 Risk factors: Intense competition from large e-commerce platforms and quick-commerce players could pressure market share and margins. Slower discretionary spending and increased customer acquisition costs may affect revenue growth and earnings performance.
 Buy: ₹ 341–346 
 Target price : ₹ 380 in two to three months 
 Stop loss : ₹ 325 
 Nifty 50 recap
 The Nifty 50 opened higher on Friday but slipped below the 23,000 mark in early trade as investors booked some profits following Thursday's sharp rally. Buyers then stepped in after the index tested its intraday low. 
 It ended the session near the day's high. The index opened at 23,065.10, touched a high of 23,149.85, a low of 22,913.80, and closed at 23,146.15, up 148.80 points (0.65%). The day's bullish candle closed near its high and above the 21-day SMA (22,861), which points to a short-term base forming near the October lows. 
 IT stocks led the gains: TECHM (+8.48%), TCS (+4.89%) and INFY (+4.61%). INDIGO (-1.91%), BSE (-1.90%), and MAXHEALTH (-1.40%) fell the most, while RELIANCE (-0.31%) weighed slightly on the index.
 The RSI has risen sharply from oversold levels to 52.81 and is well above its signal line at 34.70, so momentum is improving. The MACD line at -208.78 has crossed above its signal line at -295.98, and the histogram is positive at 87.20. This confirms a bullish crossover, although both lines remain below zero. However, the 50-, 100- and 200-day SMA are stacked in a bearish order (50 below 100, and 100 below 200). This indicates the broader trend remains weak, and the current move may be a recovery within a downtrend. 
 Immediate support is at 23,000, followed by 22,860 (the 21-day SMA) and 22,600. A break below these levels could pull the index back toward the October swing low. On the upside, 23,300 is the first resistance, followed by 23,550 (the 50-day SMA) and 23,750 (the 100-day SMA). Strong results from Tech Mahindra lifted IT stocks. Hopes of an India–U.S. trade deal, softer bond yields and easing crude prices also support the outlook. HDFCBANK, ICICIBANK, and AXISBANK report results on 17 October, so we expect the recovery to continue toward 23,550 while the index holds above 22,860.
 Nifty Bank
 On Friday, the Nifty Bank index opened higher but slipped into the red early as sellers emerged near the higher levels. Buyers came back after the index tested intraday lows, and it ended slightly higher. The index opened at 55,927.15, touched a high of 55,989.55, a low of 55,526.30, and closed at 55,844.00, up 33.50 points (0.06%). 
 The day's candle has a small body and a long lower shadow, which looks like a hammer. It shows demand above the 21-day SMA. PSU lenders led the gains: PNB (+1.09%), BANKBARODA (+1.05%) and CANBK (+1.00%). YESBANK (-3.42%), AUBANK (-1.33%), and IDFCFIRSTB (-1.25%) fell the most. Among the heavyweights, ICICIBANK, HDFCBANK, and SBIN supported the index, while INDUSINDBK and KOTAKBANK weighed on it. 
 The RSI is at 51.91. It has moved back above 50 and is well above its signal line at 40.51. The momentum is slowly turning in favour of the bulls. The MACD line at -274.60 has crossed above its signal line at -449.29, and the histogram shows positive bars at 174.69. This confirms a bullish crossover. 
 Both lines remain below zero, though, so the broader trend is only starting to recover. The index has also reclaimed the 21-day SMA (55,358). However, the 50-, 100- and 200-day SMA sit close together between 56,485 and 56

docs.title: Top 3 stocks to buy tomorrow: Mphasis, HAL, Indian Hotel by market expert; check stop-loss, target price for Mon, 19 Oct
docs.text:
The Nifty 50 climbed 2.8% over the week to 23,146.15, while the Sensex advanced 3.1% to 74,729.27, marking their best weekly performance since April 10. In Friday’s session, the Nifty gained 0.7%, while the Sensex rose 0.6%. Chandan Taparia of Motilal Oswal Financial Services, has recommended buying Mphasis, Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL) and Indian Hotels Company. He has set a target price of ₹ 2,650 for Mphasis with a stop loss at ₹ 2,425. For HAL, the target is ₹ 5,260, with a stop loss at ₹ 4,840. Indian Hotels has a target price of ₹ 815 and a stop loss at ₹ 750. On the Nifty options front, Chandan Taparia, Head Derivatives & Technicals, Wealth Management, Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd, said that the maximum call OI is at 23,100 then 23,500 strike, while maximum put OI is at 23,000 then 22,700 strike. “Call writing is seen at 23,100 then 23,150 strike while Put writing is seen at 23,100 then 23,000 strike. Option data suggests a broader trading range in between 22,700 to 23,500 zones while an immediate range between 22,900 to 23,400 levels,” said Taparia. Nifty 50 index opened on a positive note and witnessed volatile swings in the first hour before settling into a narrow range in the second half while firmly holding above 23,100 zones. The index closed near its upper band reflecting continued strength at higher levels. It formed a bullish candle on the daily frame while the weekly frame also formed a bullish candle as the index bounced from its crucial support zones and sustained its recovery at higher levels. “Now it has to hold above 23,100 zones for an up move towards 23,250 then 23,350 zones, while support can be seen at 23,000 then 22,900 zones,” said Taparia. Bank Nifty index opened on a positive note near 55,900 zones but failed to hold at higher zones and gradually drifted towards 55,500 zones in the first half of the session. docs.title: Apple Pay debuts in India: how it works, features, and key limitations
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Apple Pay debuts in India: how it works, features, and key limitations
 Ananya Grover 6 min read 18 Oct 2026, 01:08 PM IST 
 Summary
 Axis Bank credit card holders can now tap to pay using biometrics without PIN or OTP, though the launch excludes UPI integration and RuPay support. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 For iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch users in India, Apple Pay’s late-September rollout allows them to tap to pay directly via Apple’s native wallet, authenticating transactions through facial recognition or a fingerprint without needing a PIN or OTP at checkout. 
 Jennifer Bailey, vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, said at the launch in an update: “Apple Pay makes everyday payments with a card easy, secure, and private — from simply tapping to pay in stores without an extra app, PIN, or OTP to checking out online without repeatedly entering payment information.” 
 However, the feature is initially limited to Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit card holders, though reports indicate Apple is in talks with other major domestic lenders. Beyond streamlining local transactions, the service benefits international travelers who previously had to depend on physical plastic cards in India, where local UPI QR codes cannot be accessed using foreign bank accounts. Here’s everything you need to know.
 How does Apple Pay work?
 To use Apple Pay, eligible Axis Bank Visa or Mastercard credit cardholders must first add their card to Apple Wallet, either directly or through the Axis Bank mobile app. Once added, the card can be used for in-store and online purchases wherever near field communication (NFC) payments are accepted. NFC is a short-range wireless technology that enables two electronic devices to exchange small amounts of data when placed in close proximity. 
 At physical stores, users double-click the side or home button on their iPhone to open the default card in Apple Wallet, authenticate using Face ID, Touch ID, or a passcode, and hold the device near the contactless reader. The transaction is processed through the underlying credit card, meaning the card's existing billing cycle, credit limit, reward points, interest terms, and foreign transaction fees continue to apply. 
 For online purchases, Apple Pay operates on participating websites and platforms that feature it as a checkout option. Users simply select Apple Pay and authenticate via biometrics to complete the payment.
 The system relies on tokenization, ensuring the actual card number is never shared with the merchant. Instead, a device-specific token is transmitted, with biometric authentication verifying that the device owner initiated the payment. Rohit Mahajan, founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Plutos ONE said, “Biometric authentication, when combined with tokenisation and transaction-specific security controls, can offer a strong layer of protection while making payments more seamless.” He cautioned, however, that biometrics are not a silver bullet: device theft, compromised accounts and fraudulent authorisation remain risks. 
 Is contactless payment new to India?
 No. Samsung has offered tap-to-pay on its Galaxy phones since 2017, while Google Wallet, launched in May 2024, enables Android users to pay by tapping cards added to Google Pay. Although Apple Pay currently supports only Axis Bank credit cards issued on the Visa and Mastercard networks, Samsung Pay partners with major Indian banks to support both debit and credit card transactions across Visa and Mastercard networks on Galaxy devices. 
 Similarly, Google Wallet supports NFC transactions on NFC-enabled Android phones using Visa and Mastercard credit or debit cards issued by a wide network of major Indian banks. 
 Where the platforms diverge is authentication and network coverage: Apple Pay relies strictly on device biometrics (Face ID or Touch ID) for terminal taps, whereas Samsung Pay and Google Wallet require a card PIN for transactions exceeding ₹ 5,000. Furthermore, both Samsung and Google support RuPay credit cards for UPI QR code scanning, though only Google supports NFC tap-to-pay for select RuPay cards. Apple Pay currently does not support UPI or RuPay on any level. 
 Apple Pay also stands out in e-commerce checkout integration. It functions directly inside the Safari browser as a native payment option, completing purchases instantly via on-device Face ID or Touch ID. In contrast, Google Wallet requires users to select their card from an independent Google account pop-up window that works across any browser, while Samsung Pay routes authorization through an external push notification or QR code sent to the user's Galaxy phone. 
 ”Apple Pay offers ease when it comes to using (credit) cards especially for people who travel internationally and can tap and pay anywhere that accepts contactless payments,” said Rohit Mahajan, founder and CEO of plutos One. “As more people get used to it and more businesses accept it we should see more people using it for payments.” 
 What else should users know?
 According to Mukesh Pandey, founder and managing director of Rupyaapaisa.com, with OTP being out of the picture, the risk is transferred to security of the mobile device, accessibility of the account, and the chance of making unauthorized purchases if a device or a payment mechanism is hacked. He added that Indian customers must note the distinction between Apple Pay's global features and those available in India. 
 Globally, Apple Pay functions as a comprehensive digital ecosystem that replaces physical wallets by securely managing credit and debit cards, peer-to-peer cash transfers, transit passes, state IDs, and digital keys. Several of these core features are missing from the Indian rollout. First, UPI—the backbone of daily transactions in India—is not integrated. Services like Apple Cash, which enables US users to s

docs.text:
Global 
 The deadly 1.5-mile corridor that shows the fatal flaw in America’s road design
 Rebecca Cadenhead , Andrew Mollica , Audrey Valbuena , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 19 Oct 2026, 06:38 AM IST 
 Summary
 Six lanes and crosswalks a half-mile apart: How American urban-planning is failing walkers. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Bessan-Gligo stepped into the middle of the street. Moments later, a large SUV hit and killed her.
 American roads are becoming deadlier for walkers. Between 2009 and 2024, pedestrian deaths increased 72% across the U.S., federal data show. Over the same period, such deaths declined in most other developed nations, according to United Nations data. In road safety, the U.S. is an outlier.
 Pedestrian deaths are rising on certain roadways. Increasingly, people are hit by cars on roads designed like Union Avenue—all while this type of roadway continues to spread across the country.
 Union Avenue is what urbanists call a “stroad,” a fusion of “street” and “road.” A street serves as a location for destinations like businesses and homes, while a road transports people at high speeds between destinations. A “stroad” tries to do both tasks at once, said Charles Marohn, the engineer widely credited with coining the term.
 In Memphis, Union Avenue is a center of commercial activity, lined with grocery stores, fast-food restaurants and gas stations. It is also a six-lane highway that carries some 30,000 cars a day.
 The road bisected Bessan-Gligo’s life. The school she attended, Central High School, was a few blocks away from Union Avenue. In class, she was an attentive student, her history teacher said—though she was most passionate about the school’s band. High-school bands are a matter of pride across the South, and Central’s band is among the best in the nation. Bessan-Gligo played the cymbals.
 After band practice, she would begin her shift at a sandwich shop beside Union Avenue. Then she would cross it to get home. Bessan-Gligo almost always walked, a friend said; she didn’t have her driver’s license yet.
 The stores and restaurants one might find on stroads like Union Avenue, such as the sandwich shop where Bessan-Gligo worked, employ workers who often cannot afford a car. But stroads aren’t designed for pedestrians. When workers attempt to walk, they encounter a landscape built for vehicles, said Heidi Simon, a director of urban-planning at nonprofit Smart Growth America.
 Sidewalks on Union Avenue are narrow. There is no obvious place to cross the street; many intersections are located about a half-mile apart. For a driver going 40 miles an hour, a half-mile takes about 45 seconds. By foot, after a long shift, such a distance can feel like an eternity.
 Bessan-Gligo frequently crossed in the middle of Union Avenue, her friend said. She had done it so often that it no longer felt dangerous.
 In reality, this kind of crossing is especially deadly, data show. Pedestrians are most likely to be killed by cars when they cross roads “midblock”—outside of crosswalks—at night.
 Midblock crossings often surprise drivers, said Rebecca Sanders, national safety practice research lead at Fehr & Peers, a transportation consulting firm.
 Drivers can usually guide their cars down a stroad without paying attention to their periphery, she said. The design of a stroad—wide, straight, multiple lanes—facilitates speed above all else. Drivers might find themselves going faster, well past the legal limit, without realizing it.
 Meanwhile, stroads are often poorly lit at night, Sanders added. “You’d need a lot of light to light the width of a roadway that is six lanes across,” she said. By the time drivers notice a pedestrian in the road, it is often too late.
 Yet the U.S. keeps building stroads, said Nicholas Ferenchak, an associate professor at the University of New Mexico and the director of the Center for Pedestrian and Bicyclist Safety. “When you plop 200 houses down 15 miles from the place where people have to work, you have to build big roads where they can drive fast,” Ferenchak said.
 Stroads became a staple of American road design in the postwar era, he said. Urban planners assumed most people had cars, so metropolitan areas sprawled. Local and state governments built wide, multilane roads to allow people to travel to economic centers from their homes in suburbs.
 The trend continues today, particularly in the Sunbelt, now the most dangerous region of the country for pedestrians.
 Roads like Union Avenue—urban roads with speed limits of 35 mph or above—are now three times as deadly as other urban roads with lower speed limits, according to a 2022 Tennessee Department of Transportation report analyzing pedestrian fatalities in the state.
 Many stroads are also state highways, like Union Avenue. A recent study from Smart Growth America found that in 2024, 57% of all roadway fatalities occurred on state-owned roads.
 Other factors amplify stroads’ risks, said Robert Schneider, co-chair of the department of urban planning at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee. Many low-income Americans now work shifts that end late at night, when drivers find it difficult to see, he said. At the same time, Americans have gravitated in recent years toward larger vehicles, which hit pedestrians with greater force.
 Ironically, larger, heavier vehicles are often safer for the occupants of cars, Schneider said. At the same time pedestrian deaths have swelled, the number of Americans dying in car accidents has declined.
 The car that killed Bessan-Gligo was a GMC Yukon, an SUV that weighs more than 5½ thousand pounds. The car was barely damaged by the collision with her body, a police report noted. The occupants of the car—three teenage boys—walked away from the crash uninjured.

docs.title: Gold on Dhanteras: celebrate the ritual, rethink the investment
docs.text:
Mint Money Gold on Dhanteras: celebrate the ritual, rethink the investment Dhirendra Kumar (Value Research) 4 min read 18 Oct 2026, 07:01 AM IST Summary There is nothing wrong with the ritual. Just don’t mistake it for investing. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now Every year during the Diwali season, as Dhanteras comes around, people who have never bothered to invest in a planned way step out to buy gold on the same day. Jewellers stay open late, queues form at shop entrances, and almost the entire nation performs in unison what many believe is an act of investment. I’ll be careful here, because this column is about money, not culture. The Diwali season is wonderful, and Dhanteras is one of its best parts. The lamps, the cleaning of homes, the sense of a fresh beginning, the gathering of families. None of this needs improving, least of all by me. If your family welcomes prosperity by buying a little gold, buy it with all your heart. The ritual is not the problem. The problem begins when we mistake the ritual for a financial decision. Look at what is actually bought that day. For most families, it is jewellery, bought with a hefty markup in the form of ‘making charges’ that vanish into thin air as soon as you leave the shop, or coins that spend years in a bank locker that costs money to rent. Whatever else this activity may be, it will not build wealth. It is consumption, often very enjoyable consumption, but it does not become investment simply because the day is auspicious. So examine the behaviour itself. No other investment is made this way. No one wakes up on a specific day to buy mutual funds or stocks. Yet, with gold, crores of people buy on a particular date. Tell someone you plan to buy a stock on a specific day because it is auspicious, and they will tell you that you are not investing at all. The festival simply hides this absurdity under a warm glow, making behaviour we would laugh at anywhere else feel acceptable. A safety net The tradition of holding ornaments as wealth has obvious historical roots and, let’s be honest, remains relevant today, though as collateral rather than as savings. For generations of Indian families, when cash ran out, the women’s gold was the ultimate reserve. It remains high-value, credible collateral, and over the last two decades a whole lending industry has grown around it. RBI data shows that banks alone had about ₹ 5 trillion of gold jewellery loans outstanding in May 2026, roughly double the amount a year earlier. Add non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), and the total crosses ₹ 8 trillion. The gold itself is worth far more because lenders maintain a margin, lending no more than 75-85% of its value, and usually less. That puts the jewellery pledged against these loans at well over ₹ 11 trillion. Compare that with the ₹ 37.5 trillion in India's equity mutual funds , according to AMFI. The gold lying pledged in lenders’ vaults is worth close to a third of that amount. But a pledged ornament is a fallback, not an investment, and the Dhanteras reflex is best treated as a tradition, not as part of personal finance. My regular readers know that over the last couple of years, I have softened on gold and written more than once that a small allocation is good. I think of it as insurance against a world where the monetary order looks less solid than it used to, and holding gold is no longer the irrational act I once believed it was. I stand by that. But the Dhanteras purchase sits far from that logic. Insurance is bought in a form you can sell when you need it, as a small part of an overall financial plan. Dhanteras gold is bought on impulse, in the least liquid and most expensive form. Gold can be a hedge, but what you carry home from a jeweller in a fancy bag cannot play that role. Keep it separate So what should you do when Diwali is in the air, jewellery shops are glittering, and everyone around you is buying? I would say, honour the ritual as a ritual. If you love Dhanteras, buy ornaments, enjoy them, gift them, and watch them being worn with pleasure. But in your head, account for them honestly in the expenditure column, not as part of your investment plan. If you want real gold holdings, keep them in a highly liquid form that costs little to hold. Bangles or necklaces do not qualify. As I was finishing this column, most large fund houses stopped accepting fresh money into their gold funds of funds from 16 October, reportedly at Sebi’s nudge, with the rupee weak and the festive import rush ahead. You can still buy gold ETFs on the exchange if you have a demat account. The jewellers, of course, are staying open late. Global 
 A hedge-fund billionaire’s two bitter wars—against his wife and his business partner
 Peter Rudegeair , The Wall Street Journal 11 min read 19 Oct 2026, 06:47 AM IST 
 Summary
 John Overdeck is trying to prevent a feud with his wife over his $723 million divorce settlement offer from costing him in a battle with his Two Sigma co-founder. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Hedge-fund billionaire John Overdeck is going through two acrimonious breakups at once.
 One is a tabloid-worthy court battle with his estranged wife over whether the $723 million he has offered her is fair settlement for the dissolution of their nearly 24-year marriage. The other is a longer running and possibly nastier standoff with his co-founder at Two Sigma—an $85 billion quant-trading colossus—over the direction and control of the firm.
 Sitting in the witness box in a New Jersey family court on Aug. 19, with his wife Laura watching him from a few yards away, Overdeck was trying to prevent the first battle from costing him the second.
 Laura Overdeck’s lawyers were pressing the court to make public various confidential Two Sigma governance and financial records. John Overdeck, worried that any such release would supply ammunition to Two Sigma co-founder David Siegel in their battle, objected.
 Judge Bruce Buechler sounded exasperated. The only reason he could conceive why Laura Overdeck wanted the information public, he said, was to pressure her husband for a better settlement. In court the following week, the judge noted: “The court is presiding over a divorce trial between Laura Overdeck and John Overdeck. It is not presiding over a trial between, by way of example, Dr. Siegel and Mr. Overdeck.”
 Document disclosure or not, it won’t be easy for John Overdeck, 56 years old, to keep his two big problems from becoming one.
 Overdeck and Siegel have clashed for years at Two Sigma—over executive roles and compensation, succession planning and other major issues. In the process, they have lost top talent and big clients.
 His wife is seeking a cash payment equivalent to 35% of his stake in Two Sigma, or about $2.2 billion based on her lawyers’ estimate of the firm’s value. Being forced to liquidate that much of his stake to raise cash could tip control of the firm into Siegel’s favor. “Maintaining voting parity with Dr. Siegel is a principal concern,” Overdeck testified at his divorce trial last month.
 A Two Sigma spokeswoman said the firm’s assets under management are at a record high, investor demand remains strong, and the current year’s performance ranks among the its best. “We have been open with our investors about the disagreements between our co-founders and the resulting challenges,” she said.
 Some investors, though, have had enough. Among the big clients that have pulled money out is Wisconsin’s pension fund, according to people familiar with the matter and disclosures reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.
 Overdeck, a math prodigy who once worked at Amazon as Jeff Bezos’ technical assistant, and Siegel, a computer scientist with a Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, co-founded Two Sigma in 2001. The pair had worked together in the 1990s at quant hedge-fund firm D.E. Shaw Group.
 That was where John Overdeck met Laura. He proposed to her on the spring equinox of 2002, a few weeks before Two Sigma started investing with about $27 million in capital. By the time they married that October, Two Sigma’s assets under management had shot up to about $350 million.
 Like other quant firms, Two Sigma programmed its computers to sift through oceans of stock prices and other data to find patterns that helped predict where markets would move. Overdeck presided over the team of quant researchers, or modelers, who designed blueprints for trades. Siegel’s engineers constructed the underlying systems that enabled those trades to happen.
 At his divorce trial, Overdeck used a soccer analogy to describe the division of labor between Siegel and him. “I would liken the trading and modeling to the striker, or the guy who kicks the ball in the goal at the end of the play,” he said. “Investment management is very much a team sport. I was managing the very offensive end of the field.”
 The co-CEOs tried to foster a culture of nerdy comity, pitching Two Sigma as the “best place for nice geeks to work.”
 Laura Overdeck, who had a degree in astrophysics and an M.B.A., had stopped working to be a stay-at-home mom and author in Short Hills, N.J. The couple eventually had three children. Her husband later testified that he tried to stay involved, coaching the kids’ sports teams and limiting work on weekends.
 At the office, under Two Sigma’s original operating agreement, Overdeck and Siegel needed to reach consensus on most decisions. For years, that didn’t matter much because the two got along well enough. Employees often spotted them having lunch at a Mexican restaurant near Two Sigma’s headquarters in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood.
 Over time, though, they began to clash over decisions, and over who deserved credit and recognition for Two Sigma’s successes. Employees got used to walking on eggshells if there was a risk Overdeck and Siegel could perceive a slight, people familiar with the matter said. Planners of events agonized over which of the two should be asked to make opening or closing remarks, wondering if either would view one slot as inferior to the other, one of the people said.
 When the Covid-19 pandemic hit, the relationship deteriorated further, former employees said. A lengthy work-from-home period allowed conflicts to fester. Overdeck’s team of modelers and Siegel’s team of engineers bickered over how the bonus pool would be divided and which group’s job openings would take priority among Two Sigma’s recruiters.
 At home in New Jersey, the Overdecks’ nearly two-decade marriage was disint

 Insurance reforms: Why claims matter more than distribution costs
 Aprajita Sharma 7 min read 18 Oct 2026, 07:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 As Irdai weighs changes to insurance distribution, rising health claims disputes and gaps in grievance redressal underscore the need for stronger insurer accountability, fairer claims settlement and better policyholder protection. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The debate over the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (Irdai) proposed distribution reforms has centred on whether the changes could push agents and point-of-sales persons (POSPs) out of the business, hurting insurance penetration and post-sales services. But for policyholders, a more immediate question is whether their insurer will pay a valid claim, and whether they can get a fair hearing when it does.
 The numbers suggest there is considerable room for improvement. Health insurance complaints to the Insurance Ombudsman rose 263% over five years, from fiscal year 2021 (FY21) to FY25. Life insurance complaints declined 5% over the same period, though they rose 15% between FY24 and FY25. The nature of the grievances is equally telling: partial or total claim repudiation accounted for 96% of health insurance complaints, while misrepresentation of policy terms accounted for 59% of life insurance complaints.
 “Life insurance complaints may have declined partly because mis-selling, such as traditional policies being sold as fixed deposits, often comes to light only after two or three years," said Shilpa Arora, co-founder and chief operating officer, Insurance Samadhan. "While complaints can be filed with the Insurance Ombudsman within a year of the insurer rejecting them, such cases are increasingly being rejected because the policy was bought much earlier. Policyholders often discover mis-selling only when the second or third premium falls due. They have nowhere to go.”
 The outcomes of disputes raise further questions. Irdai’s distribution reform consultation paper said that in FY26, 63% of complaints disposed of through Bima Bharosa were settled in policyholders’ favour. At the Insurance Ombudsman level, the share was 75%, while 54% of cases decided by consumer forums and courts went in favour of customers.
 “These figures suggest some claims may have been unjustifiably rejected. Many policyholders may accept rejections without contesting them, and some may even lose faith in insurance altogether. Wrongful rejections fuel mistrust, and addressing them should take priority over distributor commissions,” said Kshitij Jain, co-founder, Nyvo Insurance Services.
 The focus, experts say, must extend beyond distribution to how claims are assessed, disputes resolved and insurers held accountable.
 One complaint, one system 
 A policyholder challenging a claim must navigate multiple layers of grievance redressal. The process begins with the insurer, moves to its grievance redressal officer (GRO), then to the Bima Bharosa portal and the Insurance Ombudsman, and may eventually reach consumer courts. At each stage, customers may have to resubmit documents and explain the dispute from scratch.
 “Why can't one complaint ID follow the case across all levels? Digital platforms such as Bima Sugam and Public Insurance Registry could help centralise grievance redressal. This should be a priority,” said Arora.
 Winning a dispute does not always mean a policyholder's troubles are over. Insurers must comply with an Insurance Ombudsman award within 30 days of receiving it, failing which a penalty of ₹ 5,000 per day is payable to the complainant. Yet, experts say, enforcement can be difficult, and some insurers may comply with only part of a decision.
 Arora cited cases in which insurers paid claims after the Ombudsman ruled in policyholders’ favour but subsequently cancelled their policies, preventing renewal.
 “If the Ombudsman rules that non-disclosure of a pre-existing disease (PED) was not a valid reason to reject a claim in a particular case, the insurer may still cancel the policy on the same grounds after paying the claim. We have seen multiple such cases, but policyholders cannot approach the Ombudsman again as there is no review mechanism and a fresh complaint cannot be filed under the same policy code,” she said.
 The gap extends to cases resolved through recommendations or mediation that insurers fail to honour. Customers may then have to approach consumer courts, where the time and expense involved can outweigh the amount in dispute. "Such cases fall through the system," she said.
 A mechanism to review incomplete compliance and subsequent actions linked to the same dispute could help prevent such cases from falling through the cracks.
 Make insurers pay for failures 
 When a rejected claim reaches the Ombudsman, the dispute raises questions not only about the original decision but also about the insurer’s internal grievance process. The GRO is expected to review complaints impartially, yet some disputes still escalate to external forums.
 Consumer policy expert and former member of the insurance ombudsman advisory committee Bejon Misra argued that insurers should face greater financial consequences when their decisions lead to avoidable disputes. Currently, insurers contribute towards Ombudsman-related costs based on their turnover.
 He suggested linking contributions to the number of complaints received, so insurers against which more complaints are filed bear a greater financial burden. The aim would be to encourage them to resolve genuine grievances internally rather than let them escalate.

docs.title: IMF outlook: The global economy may not be doing as badly as feared but it’s laden with major risks
docs.text:
Opinion 
 IMF outlook: The global economy may not be doing as badly as feared but it’s laden with major risks
 Daniel Moss 4 min read 18 Oct 2026, 03:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 Rarely has a fairly positive forecast from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had so many qualifiers. The predictions aren’t so much cause for celebration as a recognition that the worst hasn’t come to pass. But what can we expect from here on? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Despite everything that has been thrown at the global economy, it remains remarkably hardy. The Iran war is extracting a modest toll, higher interest rates don’t appear to have slowed growth so far, and artificial intelligence (AI) is driving an investment boom. 
 But there are limits to the staying power of the growth for which the International Monetary Fund (IMF) updated forecasts this week. Luck—and reading the right signals from markets—will play a role. 
 The expansion isn’t flawless: The sharp climb in energy prices is causing hardship, extreme weather is forcing up commodity prices and some policymakers worry about excess spending on technologies vital for data centres. Nor is it churlish to contemplate what comes next. Will the inevitable slowdown be mild, as occurred after the dotcom collapse in 2001, or deeper, like the period that followed the failure of Lehman Brothers in 2008 or the shutdowns in response to covid? 
 Central banks and fiscal authorities will again be called upon. Doing whatever it takes, however, to use the phrase deployed to great effect by former European Central Bank (ECB) president Mario Draghi, might not be so simple. 
 Budgets in several advanced economies appear close to exhaustion and bond markets are signalling their scepticism that politicians can put them on a sustainable path. France, for example, where students have taken to the streets and long-term rates have skyrocketed, would require a far bigger rescue than Portugal, Greece or a moderately sized emerging market. 
 But for now, a reckoning is still a way off. Global growth will quicken to 3.4% in 2027, the IMF projected last week, up from an estimated 3.1% this year—itself a slightly better outcome than previously anticipated. The US and China will again be the standouts: America will do a bit better than forecast and China will notch a 4% advance , unchanged from the prior forecast. France, the epicentre of a bond selloff in advanced economies, faces dimmer prospects. 
 The predictions, released at the fund’s annual meeting in Bangkok, aren’t so much cause for celebration as a recognition that the worst hasn’t come to pass. Twelve months ago, the world was still digesting steep US tariffs and traders were wringing their hands over the future of the dollar . But the ‘Sell America’ narrative fizzled and Washington’s other own goal, the jump in oil that followed its attack on Iran, hasn’t shredded the outlook. 
 Contemporary hurdles might be better understood in perspective. It takes a lot to knock growth out of the 3% vicinity. The pandemic led to a decline in world GDP of 2.7%, and the subprime meltdown pushed output slightly into negative territory. 
 Today’s nominally solid scenario depends on policymakers not making major mistakes. For now, they are saying and doing the right things. The Federal Reserve is likely to hike rates again after nudging them up last month and the ECB and central banks in India and Australia made similarly hawkish noises. In many instances, inflation remains higher than targets. 
 What happens the next time the economy gets into a really serious scrape? Who rides to the rescue? And will it be as effective as before? It will ultimately be left to central banks because governments, which control fiscal policy, are on treacherous ground. The capacity of national treasuries to borrow at competitive rates has been diminished by soaring bond yields. 
 That could be a blessing in disguise, according to Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who was finance minister during the Global Financial Crisis of 2007-09 and led the central bank before entering politics. The fixed-income upheaval provides leaders with an opportunity to put their house in order because budget compromises are often reached when dire consequences loom. 
 It’s vital this chance be seized, he said on a panel with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva at the city-state’s national university last week. Georgieva borrowed from rock legends Led Zeppelin, likening mounting debt to a “stairwell”—just not to heaven. 
 While we might not be in hell, rarely has a pretty good outlook for the global economy come with so many qualifiers. They may be more consequential than the baseline forecasts. 
 The last time the IMF held its showcase in Thailand, in 1991, the kingdom and its neighbours were on the cusp of years of runaway growth. The Soviet Union had collapsed; globalization and prosperity were the buzzwords. Few saw the currency crisis and deep recession that would envelop Asia before the decade was out. The spark was Bangkok’s decision to abandon efforts to prop up the baht. 
 Thailand’s own economy is travelling reasonably these days. Yet, like the global one, it isn’t amazing. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies.

 The Indian economy has displayed growth resilience—but fault lines have grown too that can’t be papered over
 Rajrishi Singhal 4 min read 18 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 A storm may be brewing on account of structural weaknesses that mustn’t catch policymakers off-guard. Among our worries should be growing household stashes of gold, the fallout of El Niño, generalized inflation, rising interest rates and a potential AI bubble burst. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Indian economy is in a strange spot, expected to register high growth but also vulnerable to multiple eddying currents emerging from within and outside its borders. The impact of these multiple influences—geopolitical, trade, economic, monetary or social—could see some trying times in the months ahead. 
 The Indian economy has displayed some resilience in the past and international agencies expect growth to retain buoyancy. Yet, questions are being raised whether the economy can truly weather the coming storm, especially since a procession of structural weaknesses and faultlines have queued up. 
 One minor but overlooked problem sums up the quandary in store: growing household investment in gold and silver, signifying productive resources being salted away in unproductive assets. Data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) with base year 2022-23 shows that Indian household investment in gold and silver jumped 32.3% in just the two years to 31 March 2025. 
 While updated numbers for the subsequent 18 months are not available, trade data provides some indications: gold and silver imports jumped almost 34% between 2024-25 and 2025-26. 
 Worse, in just the first three months of the current fiscal year, imports are up 37% compared with the same period last year. Admittedly, some imports are expected to find their way into value-added exports, but data shows it to be negligible so far. It may therefore be assumed that a large part of imports is finding its way into household lockers. 
 This is likely to become a speed-breaker for economic management, especially given the problems coming down the turnpike. 
 The first worry is the fallout from El Niño and the resultant deficient monsoon, 13% less than the long period average. 
 The Maharashtra government has officially declared a drought in 75% of the state: 265 of the state’s 358 talukas or tehsils . Many other states have joined in: Karnataka (226 of 240 sub-districts) and Andhra Pradesh (388 of 688 sub-districts) have also officially declared a drought. 
 Some more states are expected to follow suit. These declarations will now force state governments to provide monetary support to the rural economy, with many states looking to New Delhi for additional assistance. 
 This unplanned expenditure may force both the Centre and states to ratchet up market borrowings. The Centre, by September end, had already borrowed ₹ 813,506 crore from the market. As demands for emergency assistance go up and threaten to derail the Centre’s residual borrowing programme (nearly ₹ 7.9 trillion for October-March), the diversion of household savings to precious metals is likely to put pressure on funds availability and rates. 
 This comes on top of consumer inflation getting generalized. The argument so far was that inflationary impulses were isolated to the food and fuel items. Latest data shows that price pressures are now seeping into many other components of the price index. And while RBI recently raised its benchmark interest rates, it may have to press on the rate-hike pedal a bit harder to counter incipient inflationary pressures in the economy. 
 There is another reason why RBI’s future rate actions have become somewhat inevitable. 
 The US Federal Reserve has also jacked up interest rates, which, combined with interest rate increases by other central banks across the world, signals the end of an era marked by abundant liquidity, low benchmark interest rates, bulging central bank balance sheets and cheap financing. 
 This has, among other reasons, unnerved foreign portfolio investors, and they have repatriated close to $27 billion so far from Indian markets this calendar year. 
 Logic says that fresh currency inflows thanks to a souped-up foreign deposit scheme and foreign investment into IDBI Bank should act as a counterfoil to surging outflows. And yet, RBI recently introduced harsh measures to stop a slide in the rupee value, somewhat like bringing a bazooka to a fistfight. As a next step, RBI is likely to push hard on its interest rate buttons. 
 The existing package of geopolitical conflicts, volatile energy prices, elevated inflationary pressures and rising interest rates could get a further shock from the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble bursting. 
 The gargantuan volumes of investment into AI companies could stop abruptly if AI-related profits and productivity gains fall short of expectations. This could detonate a chain of collapses and bankruptcies that could reverberate across the global economy, including India’s. While the AI-related investment spree has largely bypassed the country, there would be no escaping its second-order effects. 
 As inflation and interest rates rise in a stressed economy where jobs and real wages have been shrinking, more savings might get diverted to shiny metals. This is not an ideal situation. During times of crisis, financial savings provide stability; they act as a buffer against adverse economic events by allowing households to finance consumption without having to borrow at above-normal rates. 
 While households can still leverage their gold and silver to borrow from the financial system, as has been happening over the past few years, it has the potential to increase indebtedness and financial stress. 
 Growing bullion savings sends another signal: households are either left with no alternative saving avenues or lack confidenc

docs.title: The AI stock market wobble is a reminder: This time isn’t different
docs.text:
Global 
 The AI stock market wobble is a reminder: This time isn’t different
 James Mackintosh , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 19 Oct 2026, 06:41 AM IST 
 Summary
 The artificial intelligence build-out hasn’t shown it can avoid the problems of past massive capital projects, such as railways and the internet. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 AI stocks have had a terrible few days as hot inflation raises the cost of finance and threatens the debt-fueled investment in data centers. Investors showed they are alive to one of the big risks in AI, that hopes for trillions of dollars of capital spending might be derailed. An even bigger risk: construction continues at full speed.
 Extraordinary profits help obscure both risks and reassure many of those buying stocks.
 The profits aren’t a mirage. But they should only reassure us if we can rely on what legendary financier John Templeton said were the four most dangerous words in investing: “This time it’s different.”
 The AI build-out hasn’t yet shown it can avoid the problems of past massive capital projects, such as railways and the internet. At least so far, this time isn’t different.
 Start with the profits. Capital expenditure, or capex, by one company generates revenue for other companies. The data-center boom is creating massive revenue elsewhere. Makers of everything AI needs have been able to jack up prices for chips, cooling equipment, cables, backup generators, turbines and a host of other supplies, boosting profit margins as sales soar.
 But this is temporary. Once the build-out is complete in a few years, capital spending will drop drastically, as maintenance, repair and upgrades are cheaper than a whole new building.
 Investors understand this, and the debate is primarily over how long profits can stay high, not whether they can stay high. This can be seen in the share prices. Yes, they’ve gone up, but the gains have been modest when you consider the huge surge in profits. Investors know much of the profit is temporary.
 The result is that while prices have gone up, valuations, measured as the price-to-forecast-earnings ratio, have gone down. Investors are paying less per dollar of the earnings coming up in the next year, because they know it won’t last.
 The valuation of Nvidia, the most valuable U.S. company, has dropped from 23 times predicted earnings to 15 times, even as its shares rose 15%, and memory-chip stock Micron trades at a forward PE ratio of just under five times after its shares tripled.
 “To me the market doesn’t have a P problem, it has an E problem,” says Rob Almeida, global investment strategist at MFS Investment Management.
 Some think this is so extreme it is a bubble in earnings, the E part of the PE ratio. If earnings deflate, elevated valuations will become obvious.
 Gerard Minack of Minack Advisors points out that forecast earnings for the eight biggest AI stocks—Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and Palantir—plus what he calls the “next 11” AI players, have increased by $700 billion this year, against an increase of less than $500 billion for the rest of the S&P 500.
 Bulls can take comfort that investors understand that amazing earnings won’t last. Bears can say froth in earnings explains why PE ratios haven’t soared the way they usually do in a bubble, and look at measures that try to smooth cyclical highs and lows, such as the Shiller price-to-10-years’-earnings ratio. There’s also a parallel to 2007, when the bubble in bank stocks (usually valued by comparison to balance sheet, rather than earnings) was hidden by overstated book values.
 This past week the threat to capex-related profits became obvious, as higher-than-expected inflation drove up financing costs and so threatened the AI construction boom. Shares in CoreWeave, an independent data-center operator, plunged 24% to wipe out all gains this year, those in memory-chip maker Micron dropped 11% and its South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix tumbled twice as much. Other AI suppliers also fell hard.
 The moves show just how much it will hurt if the AI capex doesn’t materialize.
 Yet, if the falls prove merely another brief interlude in the raging AI bull market and construction continues as expected, it will be just as risky—in a different way. Spending $9 trillion on AI by 2032, as Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimated in a Brookings paper recently, would make it the biggest U.S. capital project ever, at 3.2% of GDP a year.
 For this to work out for investors, we have to get past the temporary capex-related profits to generate sustainable AI profits. That means finding worthwhile uses that increase productivity enough that customers are willing to pay the full cost of developing and using the technology. If it disappoints, much of that $9 trillion will have been wasted.
 The lessons from historical capital-spending booms offer both good and bad news. The good news is that mostly they delivered as much as or more than expected, with huge benefits for society. The bad news is that, from the canal mania of 1790s England, the British railway bubble of the 1840s, its American equivalent in the 1880s, electrification, radio, television and up to the fiber build-out of the dot-com bubble, investors were sorely disappointed.
 It took too long for the benefits to be realized, profits were smaller and came later than hoped or competition meant excess profits flowed to the users of the new technology, not its owners. AI is vulnerable to each of these. Investors really need this time to be different.

docs.title: Mutual funds’ portfolio shifts: Aditya Infotech, BSE stand out among top 10 stocks by holding value changes in September
docs.text: If you invest in mutual funds, it is worth tracking which stocks fund managers are buying and selling, as these changes can offer insights into how their portfolios are shifting.In September 2026, mutual funds increased the value of their holdings in stocks such as BSE, HDFC Bank, Coal India, Meesho, and Gland Pharma, according to the latest Fund Folio – Indian Mutual Fund Tracker report by Motilal Oswal Financial Services. However, a rise in the value of a mutual fund's holdings does not necessarily mean fund managers bought more shares. The change can reflect fresh purchases, changes in share prices, or a combination of both.Comparing changes in holding value with changes in shareholding quantity offers investors a clearer picture of where mutual funds increased their exposure.Which stocks saw the biggest increase in mutual funds’ holding value in September?Aditya Infotech recorded the highest growth in holding value among the top 10 stocks, at 35.6%, while BSE led in the percentage increase in shareholding quantity, at 34.6%.BSE saw a 26.8% increase in the value of mutual funds' holdings to ₹20,060 crore. The quantity of shares held rose 34.6%, while the stock's price declined 5.8% during the month. This indicates that the increase in holding value was driven by a higher number of shares held, rather than a rise in the stock price.Aditya Infotech also recorded a substantial increase in holding value, up 35.6% to ₹6,070 crore. Its shareholding quantity rose 25.7%, while its stock price gained 7.5%. Both the increase in shareholding and price appreciation contributed to the higher portfolio value.However, HDFC Bank's holding value increased by just 1% to ₹2.8 lakh crore, alongside a 1% rise in the quantity of shares held. Its price was nearly unchanged, suggesting that the increase in holding value largely reflected the additional shares.ITC presents another example of why investors should compare value and quantity. Mutual funds' holding value rose 3%, while their shareholding increased only 0.1%. The stock's 2.9% price gain explains most of the increase in value.How many mutual funds bought or sold these stocks in September?Tata Steel recorded the broadest buying participation, with 19 funds buying and 2 selling. Dr Reddy’s Laboratories followed, with 17 funds buying against four selling. BSE and HDFC Bank each saw 15 funds buying, exceeding the number of funds selling.ITC saw a more mixed pattern, with 11 funds buying and 10 selling. Aditya Infotech, which recorded the highest growth in holding value, saw 10 funds buying and 6 selling.Disclaimer: This is purely for educational/informational purposes and should not be taken as any sort of investment advice. Always consult a SEBI-registered advisor before making any investment decisions.

 Putin floats a summit with Trump and Xi to decide Ukraine’s fate
 Lingling Wei , Alex Leary , Thomas Grove , Josh Dawsey , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 19 Oct 2026, 06:24 AM IST 
 Summary
 The Russian leader is trying to capitalize on warming ties with the president to unlock a favorable resolution to the war with Kyiv. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio

 Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed that he, President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about Ukraine in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year conflict that would favor Moscow, said people familiar with the discussions.
 The plan represents an effort by Putin to capitalize on warming ties between Trump and the Russian leader that have alarmed Ukraine and its allies in Washington and Europe. Such a summit—one without the involvement of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky—would be unprecedented and send alarm bells ringing in European capitals and beyond.
 Putin floated the idea in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, said a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. That conversation also produced a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale on the global market.
 Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions were taking place over a potential meeting.
 “There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told The Wall Street Journal.
 A senior U.S. official said Trump hadn’t agreed to such a summit. Still, the official said the president could be receptive to the idea, given his desire to fulfill a campaign promise to settle the war. Trump had said it would be finished on “day one” of his new term, but he is now approaching nearly two years in office.
 The Kremlin has suggested holding the trilateral dialogue on the sidelines of the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the people familiar with discussions said. That gathering takes place on Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese tech hub.
 A potential three-way dialogue on Chinese soil would mark a big step for Xi in his efforts to elevate China’s role as a diplomatic power broker, said analysts who study China. Russian officials proposed the idea to Beijing through diplomatic channels and the Chinese side has indicated it wouldn’t object if Trump is on board, said other people close to recent discussions between Moscow and Beijing.
 “China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the U.S. and Russia,” said Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank.
 The White House and Chinese Embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
 Putin has proposed a trilateral summit to both Trump and Xi on previous occasions, the former Russian intelligence officer said. This time, however, it comes during a reversal of Moscow’s fortunes with Washington.
 Trump just notched a deal with Putin to get Russian diesel in a bid to lower fuel prices that have slowed the American economy and hurt Republican prospects ahead of the midterm elections. On Friday, Trump halted implementation of sanctions that were to be imposed on Russia under a bipartisan bill he signed last month, drawing criticism from lawmakers, including some of his allies.
 The senior White House official said Trump made the decisions after seeing few other good options to lower prices.
 The consensus among energy experts is that the Iran war is the primary cause of rising diesel prices and that the amount of fuel Russia has promised to sell wouldn’t move the market much.
 At the same time, Trump has shown renewed frustration with Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader must stop strikes on Russian refineries and suggesting that the country needs a new president. U.S.-led efforts to broker an end to the war, meanwhile, have been largely stalled.
 In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump took aim at Zelensky, following Ukraine’s strike on an oil terminal in Putin’s hometown of St. Petersburg earlier in the day. He accused the Ukrainian leader of targeting Russian diesel refineries and said he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
 Trump said he was holding off on imposing sanctions because he didn’t want to drive Russia away from the bargaining table. “I WANT THIS WAR END!” he wrote.

The format also excludes from the picture Europe, which the Kremlin sees as its main obstacle to clinching victory in Ukraine.
 The former Russian intelligence officer said Putin has broad, if unrealistic, ambitions for the trilateral format as a second Yalta summit, which would divide up the globe into spheres of influence.
 Even if Xi and Trump are unlikely to agree to that, the image of the American, Russian and Chinese leaders negotiating the fate of one nation would be a powerful signal. docs.title: 8th Pay Commission: What is the difference between basic pay, grade pay and pay level? Expert explains
docs.text:
In these meetings held across the country over the last few months, eligible employee unions and associations have tabled their views, grievances, and aspirations on core aspects such as basic pay, grade pay, and pay levels. Along with fitment factors, pension reforms and associated aspects. 
 Now, it is vital for serving central government employees, associated stakeholders and pensioners to clearly acknowledge that each of the terms discussed above has a distinct meaning and role in determining an employee’s salary. Having a clear understanding of these terms is particularly significant as employees await the 8th Pay Commission's recommendations on revised pay and pensions. 
 For example, the prominent employee union, i.e., the Staff Side of the National Council (Joint Consultative Machinery) (NC-JCM), has requested that the 8th Pay Commission panel provide employees with a minimum basic pay of ₹ 69,000. This has been requested on a fitment factor of 3.833. 
 In the 6th and the 7th pay commissions, the officially approved fitment factors were 1.86 and 2.57, respectively. This time, the unions are pushing for a higher multiplier to ensure that serving central government employees and pensioners can meaningfully combat rising inflation. With these basics in mind, let us discuss the fundamental differences among basic pay , grade pay, and pay levels. 
 Basic pay is the core component of an employee’s salary, excluding allowances such as Dearness Allowance (DA) and House Rent Allowance (HRA). These allowances are generally calculated using basic pay as the reference. The amount varies according to the employee’s pay level, inflation trend and position in the pay structure. 
 Grade pay, on the other hand, is slightly different; it was introduced under the 6th Pay Commission. It was added to the pay band to reflect an employee’s position and seniority. However, the 7th Pay Commission discontinued the grade pay system and introduced a pay matrix with 18 levels, making it easier to determine salaries and increments. 
 Adhil Shetty, CEO, BankBazaar, explained the difference between basic pay, grade pay and pay level in detail, stating, “Basic pay is the core component of a government employee’s salary and the base on which allowances such as DA and HRA are calculated. Grade pay was introduced under the 6th Pay Commission to denote seniority within a pay band. The 7th Pay Commission replaced this structure with a pay matrix of 18 pay levels. For instance, Level 1 starts at ₹ 18,000, while Level 7 begins at ₹ 44,900. Under the 8th Pay Commission , the final fitment factor will be key in determining the revised basic pay across each of these levels.” 
 Currently, the 8th Pay Commission is preparing for a key meeting in Mumbai starting on 22 October 2026. Since its constitution on 3, November 2025, the 8th Pay Commission has held several important discussions in various states and Union Territories, including Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Ladakh, and West Bengal. 
 As per the Terms of Reference (ToR) , the three-member 8th Pay Commission headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai has been given 18 months to submit its final report to the central government. The tentative date for submitting the final report is around May-June 2027. 
 The recommendations of the 8th Pay Commission can lead to changes in the existing pay structure, allowances, basic pay, and fitment factor multiplier, depending on the final decisions, internal calculations and cost assessments. 
 Still, the revised salary cannot be determined until the government accepts and implements the final recommendations of the 8th Pay Commission. Employees should therefore treat proposed fitment factors and projected salary figures until the final report is tabled as estimates rather than confirmed increases.
