docs.title: ₹50,000 in KVP vs ₹50,000 in NSC: Which post office scheme is better for a five-year goal? Check out the calculations
docs.text:
Both of these schemes are government-backed, predictable in nature, and offer investors clearly defined savings options. Still, their interest rates, maturity periods, terms of investment, and tax benefits differ. 
 That is why, for someone who aspires to invest and plans to redeem the funds exactly 5 years later, the NSC scheme is generally considered the more suitable option. This is because this investment option matures within that period only. 
 On the other hand, Kisan Vikas Patra (KVP) is generally the more prudent option for aspiring investors who are willing to stay invested and keep their funds invested for longer and want to double their investment at maturity. Let us now look at the calculations and a clear comparison between the two investment options for better understanding and clarity. 
 For the October-December 2026, quarter, NSC offers an interest rate of 7.7% per annum, whereas KVP offers 7.5% per annum . In both schemes, the rate of interest is compounded yearly. The salient features of the schemes are elaborated below: 
 Note: The maturity amounts are approximate. The interest rates above are subject to change as per government directives. NSC interest is compounded annually, while KVP doubles the investment at maturity under the applicable scheme terms. 
 Now, it is a given that KVP offers a higher total interest rate between the two schemes; still, it takes about 9 years and 7 months to double the investment. This makes it unsustainable for someone who needs the funds in 5 years. NSC meanwhile provides investors with a defined 5-year investment horizon. 
 In case your goal is to build a fund for educational expenses, a planned purchase or another financial requirement due in the next 5 years, then NSC can generally cater well and can be a better fit. It also offers investors a fixed maturity period and may also qualify for a deduction under Section 80C , subject to applicable tax rules, regulations and the chosen tax regime. 
 KVP, on the other hand, can be a prudent option for investors who have a longer investment horizon and do not require immediate access to their funds. Still, its longer maturity period is an important consideration that should not be overlooked while planning personal finances. 
 It is also vital to keep in mind that the interest earned under both schemes is taxable under the applicable income tax rules . Your post-tax return may therefore be lower than the amount discussed in the calculations above. 
 In summary, for a 5-year financial goal, NSC is the more practical and prudent investment option. KVP may be worth considering if your priority is long-term capital growth and you can stay invested until maturity. 
 Furthermore, before you invest in any investment option or scheme, it is wise to sit down with a certified financial advisor and plan your investments in line with your long-term financial goals. Any investment decisions should be made only after gaining a clear understanding of the basic principles of small savings schemes and after a discussion with a certified financial advisor. 
 Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and should not be considered investment or tax advice. Verify the latest Post Office scheme rules, interest rates and applicable conditions before investing, and consult a qualified expert to assess your individual circumstances.

docs.title: Have a minor PAN card? Here's how to update it to major status with new photo and signature after turning 18
docs.text:
A PAN card issued before the age of 18 remains valid after an individual becomes an adult, but the details need to be updated to reflect their status as a major. The process involves updating an existing PAN record, not applying for an entirely new PAN number. Here's what you need to know. A minor PAN card is issued to an individual below 18 years of age. It serves as a tax identification document and is required when financial activities, such as certain investments or transactions, are undertaken in the child’s name. Since a minor cannot independently complete all formalities, a parent or legal guardian handles the application. The minor’s PAN is linked to the child’s identity, although the application and contact details belong to the parent. It is not mandatory for every child to have a minor PAN. The first step is to check the information printed on your PAN card and the details recorded in your PAN application. You can submit a request through the official Protean eGov or UTIITSL PAN service to make changes or corrections in existing PAN data. No. Turning 18 does not require you to obtain another PAN. A person must not hold more than one PAN. If you already have a PAN issued during childhood, use the existing number when requesting changes to the record. Once the correction request is processed, you can receive a PAN card reflecting the updated details while retaining the same PAN number. Disclaimer: This is for informational purposes only.  How Zelensky decided to take the risk and publicly confront Trump
 Marcus Walker , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 18 Oct 2026, 12:22 PM IST 
 Summary
 The Ukrainian leader is calling out the White House for relaxing pressure on Russia, drawing more ire.

 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was on an overnight train and in a gloomy mood when he decided to take the gloves off with President Trump.
 News reached Zelensky and his advisers on the train from Kyiv to Poland late on Tuesday that Russian missiles had pounded Kyiv without the usual U.S. warning of a missile launch for the second day in a row, according to a person present.
 In recent days, Trump had eased energy sanctions on Moscow, praised Russian President Vladimir Putin, piled pressure on Ukraine and called for Zelensky’s removal. The Ukrainian president feared more concessions to Moscow were coming, the person said.
 For 18 months, since a disastrous Oval Office meeting with Trump early in his presidency, Zelensky had been trying to court him. Now he signaled to those around him that plain speaking was needed, the person said.
 Zelensky, traveling to meet European allies in London and Brussels, decided to publicly criticize Trump’s approach, despite the risk of angering him further. He wanted to send a message to the public in the U.S. and Europe: Ukraine would defend itself however it needed to, and it wasn’t to blame for Russia’s invasion or for high global fuel prices.
 The Ukrainian leader used scheduled interviews with British media on Wednesday to criticize Trump’s expressed preference for dealing with Putin and moves to relax economic sanctions on Moscow. “I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Trump said this week.
 Putin “is a real evil of today,” Zelensky told the Financial Times. “How can Trump be friends with him? I think that it’s a mistake. It’s his choice again and again.”
 “Americans are on our side,” he said, appealing to the country beyond the White House. “I know that the majority of the United States supports Ukraine.”
 Zelensky’s pushback follows the arc of other European allies’ dealings with the American president since his return to the White House. A series of clashes over trade, the Russia-Ukraine war, the future of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the U.S. war with Iran and threats to seize the Danish territory of Greenland have led even once-close political allies in European capitals to distance themselves from Trump this year.
 “I don’t know why the U.S. president behaves this way towards his own allies,” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in June when he made disparaging remarks about her. “It’s a pity that he doesn’t have the same determination with the enemies of the West, with the enemies of the United States, with whose leadership he shows himself to be much more accommodating.”
 Like Meloni and others in Europe, Zelensky risks further blowback from Trump for criticizing him. But the stakes for Ukraine are far higher.
 Europe’s poorest country, locked in the fifth year of a war of survival against Russia’s attempted conquest, receives valuable U.S. support in three areas : intelligence-sharing, Starlink contracts, and sales of U.S. weapons and ammunition to Europe for use in Ukraine.
 Trump cut virtually all other U.S. support for Ukraine in early 2025. Europe has since provided the bulk of Ukraine’s military and financial aid, but it can only partially replace American satellite and intelligence capabilities. Washington is also a crucial part of the Western sanctions regime that keeps economic pressure on Russia.
 That sanctions policy is threatening to fray. Trump this month announced a deal with Putin to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets, saying it would help bring down diesel prices. Then, on Friday, he waived most sanctions against Russia that were set to be levied under a bipartisan bill he signed last month.
 The moves drew bipartisan criticism for weakening economic pressure on Moscow. Energy experts say the announced amounts of Russian diesel are too small to make much difference and the U.S.-Iran war has been the dominant driver of high global fuel prices this year.
 Earlier on Oct. 9, just before Trump announced the diesel deal, Zelensky had held amicable discussions in Kyiv with a group of U.S. lawmakers who support Ukraine, led by Sen. Roger Wicker (R., Miss.), chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.
 Republicans in the delegation had floated an idea with Ukrainian officials that the U.S. could give Ukraine access to Starlink up to around 200 miles deep inside Russia, so that its drones could hunt Russian ballistic-missile launchers. Ukraine can’t currently use Starlink inside Russia. In return, Kyiv could stop bombing Russian refineries, they said, according to Sen. Kevin Cramer (R., N.D.). Zelensky agreed it was a good idea, he said.
 In Miami on the same day, however, White House negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner pressed Ukrainian officials to stop hitting refineries with no quid pro quo, according to several participants in the meeting. The Americans repeatedly said they were giving Kyiv valuable intelligence, which Ukrainian and European officials present read as an implicit warning that it could be curtailed. U.S. officials deny any threat was made.

 Quick commerce, uncertain demand push up festive borrowing for consumer brands

 Summary
 Consumer brands are borrowing 15-20% more this festive season.

 Direct-to- consumer (D2C) brands are stepping up working-capital financing during the festive season, as uncertain demand and the need to meet peak sales put pressure on cash flows. 
 Growth capital among D2C businesses typically rises by up to 35% during the festive quarter. This year, too, borrowings by consumer brands are roughly 15-20% higher year-on-year as businesses navigate demand uncertainty, according to executives Mint spoke with.
 While established companies have greater access to bank credit and internal cash flows, emerging brands turn to specialist lenders.
 Mumbai-based revenue-based financing platform GetVantage has seen 120% year-on-year growth and is targeting ₹ 200-240 crore in festive-season disbursements. Debt-financing platform Recur Club has announced a ₹ 500 crore fund for D2C brands and facilitated around ₹ 275 crore for more than 100 such brands in the current fiscal year.
 The funds are being used for inventory, marketing and faster replenishment across sales channels.
 “The festive season can make or break a D2C brand's year, and this year the pressure is higher,” said Eklavya Gupta, co-founder of Recur Club. Brands must stock inventory across more channels as quick commerce takes a larger share of D2C sales, he said, while avoiding excessive commitments before demand becomes clearer. 
 A survey by the community social media and civic engagement platform LocalCircles, based on more than 67,000 responses across 307 districts, released on 15 October, estimated that urban Indian households’ festive discretionary spending would fall 6% to ₹ 1.97 trillion this year, from ₹ 2.1 trillion in 2025. The report cited persistent inflation, rising borrowing costs, and the absence of last year’s goods and services tax (GST) rate-cut boost. 
 Quick-commerce cost 
 A shift towards quick commerce is adding to brands’ inventory requirements. Anmol Sahai Mathur, vice-president of marketing at MARS Cosmetics, said stock in a central warehouse is of little use if a product is unavailable at the location fulfilling a customer’s order. Maintaining inventory across more locations can increase working-capital needs, though faster replenishment and stock turnover can offset some of the costs.
 “Quick commerce has turned availability into the product,” said Garima Kakkar, co-founder of V3 Ventures-backed fragrance brand Fraganote, pointing to the risk of losing customers when products are unavailable on Blinkit and Zepto during peak gifting periods. 
 Chocolate maker Smoor said the channel has increased its working-capital requirements only modestly, as faster stock turnover offsets more frequent replenishment. 
 Quick commerce contributes around 20% of business at tea and wellness company Vahdam India and about 8% at Smoor. 
 Faster sales, however, do not always mean faster cash realization. Fraganote said quick-commerce platforms require stocks across multiple locations, while marketplaces have fulfilment and settlement timelines, and offline retail involves longer credit cycles. “These differences affect how much cash brands must tie up in operations,” Kakkar noted. 
 “Real-time data from digital channels is creating opportunities for cash-flow-based financing, allowing lenders to align working-capital facilities with business performance rather than relying solely on collateral,” said Bhavik Vasa, founder and chief executive of GetVantage. 
 Treading with caution 
 Despite the need to stock up, brands are prioritizing proven products and making smaller initial commitments to less predictable festive offerings. 
 At Smoor, last year’s sales and the current channel mix guide inventory decisions. Its in-house manufacturing allows it to replenish products during the season rather than commit to the entire requirement upfront. The company said its inventory days are already below last year’s levels. 
 Mars Cosmetics is also making commitments in stages where supplier lead times allow, using early sales signals to adjust replenishment and prioritizing established sellers. 
 Fraganote is buying established fragrances with confidence, but starting with smaller quantities of new Diwali gift sets. It tracks early sales and reorders products that perform well. Slower-moving fragrances can also be sold through other channels beyond the festive period, Kakkar said. 
 Marketing adds to the demand for working capital. Fraganote is spending more on visibility and product discovery on quick-commerce platforms rather than deep discounting. Vahdam India is similarly focusing on awareness and channel-specific marketing instead of relying entirely on promotions. 
 Repayment cycles have so far remained unaffected, GetVantage’s Vasa said, noting that these loans typically have shorter tenures and more frequent repayments than conventional business loans.
 “But, if festive demand falls short of expectations, lenders may need to marginally extend grace periods to give brands more time to generate cash from inventory,” he added.
 “With a large share of households relying on savings to fund festive purchases, the key question is how sustainable this spending momentum will be beyond the festive season. Consumer brands will need to distinguish between a temporary seasonal surge and demand that can be sustained in the months ahead,” said Sachin Taparia, founder and chief executive officer of LocalCircles.

docs.title: Autumn skincare: How to protect your skin from dryness and pollution
docs.text:
Lounge 
 Autumn skincare: How to protect your skin from dryness and pollution
 Shahnaz Husain 4 min read 18 Oct 2026, 01:14 PM IST 
 Summary
 Shahnaz Husain shares ways to tackle seasonal dullness, restore moisture and keep skin supple as the weather changes 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Autumn brings more than a change in temperature. As humidity drops and pollution levels rise in many Indian cities, skin can become more prone to dryness, irritation and dullness.
 The shift from summer to winter is a good time to reassess your skincare routine. Focus on gentle cleansing, adequate moisturising and protecting the skin’s natural barrier rather than simply adding more products.
 Understand Your Skin’s Needs 
 Look out for common seasonal skin concerns, including dryness and rough patches, particularly around the cheeks and lips. Your skin may also feel tight after cleansing or bathing, while dehydration and the buildup of dead skin cells can leave your complexion looking dull. Increased sensitivity, redness and flaking are other signs that your skin may need extra care.
 Recognising these changes can help you adapt your skincare routine to the season rather than relying on the same products all year round.
 Gentle Cleansing
 Cleansing helps remove sweat, dirt, excess oil and sunscreen, but harsh face washes can strip the skin of its natural oils, leaving it feeling dry and uncomfortable. Opt for a gentle cleanser formulated with aloe vera, which can help soothe the skin while cleansing without leaving it feeling stripped.
 During autumn, wash your face in the morning and evening, adjusting the frequency to your skin's needs. Avoid harsh soaps and aggressive exfoliation, which can compromise the skin barrier, and gently pat your face dry with a soft towel instead of rubbing it.
 Moisturising is essential for keeping skin soft and supple as the weather cools. A good moisturiser helps reduce water loss and supports the skin's natural protective barrier, keeping dryness and tightness at bay.
 Natural ingredients can complement your skincare routine by helping soften the skin, retain moisture and ease dryness. Shea butter, honey, coconut oil and oatmeal each offer different benefits, but choosing the right ingredient depends on your skin type and concerns.
 Shea butter: Rich in emollient fats, shea butter helps soften rough skin and reduce moisture loss. It is particularly useful for dry areas such as the elbows, hands and legs.
 Honey: A natural humectant, honey helps attract and retain moisture. It can be used in a rinse-off mask, although it may cause irritation in some people with sensitive skin.
 Coconut oil: Coconut oil helps reduce moisture loss and soften very dry skin. However, it may clog pores in some people, making it a better option for dry body areas than acne-prone facial skin.
 Oatmeal: Colloidal oatmeal, a finely ground form of oats used in skincare formulations, can help soothe dry, itchy skin and support the skin’s protective barrier. Look for products specifically formulated with colloidal oatmeal.
 Besides topical skincare, a balanced diet rich in vitamins, antioxidants and essential fatty acids can also support healthy-looking skin. Include seasonal fruits and vegetables, nuts and seeds in your meals, and stay hydrated.
 Dead skin cells can build up on the skin’s surface, leaving it looking dull and feeling rough. Gentle exfoliation can help improve texture, but overdoing it may irritate the skin and compromise its natural barrier. Avoid harsh homemade scrubs, particularly those made with sugar, and opt for a gentle exfoliating product suited to your skin type.
 If your skin is dry or sensitive, choose a mild formula and use it sparingly. Avoid exfoliating skin that is irritated or inflamed, and follow with a moisturiser. If you experience persistent redness, burning or increased flaking, stop using the product.
 Daily Sun Protection
 Cooler weather does not eliminate the need for sunscreen. UV exposure can contribute to premature ageing, pigmentation and skin cancer throughout the year. Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher every morning to exposed skin, and reapply approximately every two hours when outdoors, or sooner after swimming or sweating.
 A Quick Guide
 A consistent routine is often more effective than layering multiple products. As the weather changes, focus on keeping your skin clean, moisturised and protected.
 Morning: Cleanse gently, apply a moisturiser suited to your skin type and finish with broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher.
 Evening: Remove make up and sunscreen, cleanse without stripping the skin of its natural oils, and apply a moisturiser to replenish hydration.
 The key to healthy-looking skin through autumn is not an elaborate routine but a few thoughtful adjustments that help maintain moisture, protect the skin barrier and address your skin’s changing needs.
 Shahnaz Husain is the founder of the Shahnaz Husain Group of Companies.

docs.text:
Opinion 
 Long-term capital gains and securities transaction taxation: Here’s how to reform them
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 19 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 India’s finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman has hinted at a possible review of these levies that many market participants consider a bugbear. Lighter levies are popular, but tax principles must guide reforms. Here’s what the next budget could do. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Come budget time and demands for concessions, special interest giveaways, tax cuts and so on start filling up the finance minister’s inbox. Lobbies get particularly active during this period, preparing white papers for their clients, submitting briefing notes to key bureaucrats or ministers and courting the media to amplify their voice. 
 The finance ministry convenes separate meetings with economists, industry representatives, agriculturists, medium-and- small-scale sector leaders, bank chiefs and executives from the broader financial sector. All their proposals and pleas are heard, discussed, recorded and compiled. 
 Some outlandish demands are binned even before the day is over. But most suggestions are put through a filter, assessed for budgetary impact and then either discarded or moved to a shortlist.
 Most years, a particular demand tops the list and turns into a talking point. This year, given the sharp fall in stock market indices, there have been calls to review the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax and securities transaction tax (STT), both of which are widely seen as put-offs for investors.
 Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman, to her credit, did not dismiss the idea of a relook out of hand, saying a debate over these levies was healthy and she would hear stakeholders out. Markets responded positively to this gesture. 
 There has long been a measure of discontent over how stock market participation is taxed. The STT was introduced in 2004 after the LTCG tax was retired, imposing a tiny levy on each market trade in lieu of tax-free long-term gains. 
 Oddly, though, STT stayed after LTCG tax was re-imposed on equity in 2018; as a result, investors now pay tax both on trades and gains. This came after civil society clamoured that nil LTCG tax was a privilege for India’s privileged. 
 In 2024, its rate was upped from 10% to 12.5%. STT on derivatives has risen too. Differential tax treatment between equity and debt mutual funds has also been a concern. But then, we cannot overlook the revenue angle. Both levies mop up about ₹ 2 trillion every year, so the Centre may be reluctant to let that go, especially in these volatile times. 
 There might be a way out of this impasse. 
 An important school of thought posits that developing nations like India should design taxation to meet broader development objectives. The caveat: any concessions should be aptly targeted, limited and not overwhelm tax administration or undermine revenue collection. 
 The finance ministry could examine a case for reforms that treats debt and equity mutual funds alike. Right now, the system reveals a bias for a specific asset class: equity. A lighter burden on debt funds held by those whose income is in upper tax slabs will be critical if and when India’s private sector dials up its capital expenditure. Perhaps a rate rationalization of LTCG levies could cheer equity markets as well. 
 As for the STT, it needs a different approach. The levy originally looked like a Tobin tax, meant to temper market volatility. Like all cesses and surcharges, however, it has become a permanent levy applied to all market participants; STT could be deployed only to stem retail losses in the derivatives segment, or, more broadly, as a tool to contain red-hot speculation should it threaten market disruption. 
 India currently faces a savings and investment distortion at the household level; the classical solution to that has always been through taxation structures.

 Manu Joseph: The poor have a right to fun—why don't the rich understand that?
 Manu Joseph 5 min read 18 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 The perception of the elite that frivolity is a form of luxury, and that the poor are or should be preoccupied with dreary things is one of our worst misdiagnoses of the human condition. Entertainment is not the byproduct of progress—rather, progress is a byproduct of entertainment. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A few days ago, when Elon Musk appeared to realize that India was not opening its vast market to his Starlink, he insulted the government and suggested Mukesh Ambani was sabotaging his satcom plans. 
 He said another thing, which was the most dubious part of his lament, yet it would be perceived as his strongest argument in favour of a company that beams the internet from space: “There are many areas of India… with no internet access, which denies children the opportunity for education… Starlink would change their lives for the better… [It] has proven to be essential for saving lives during natural disasters throughout the world.” 
 This is spurious not because he doesn’t care about the poor. Maybe he does; who doesn’t care for the poor, it costs nothing. It is spurious for a more complex reason. Every time a tech savant wants to flog his stuff in India, he feels he has to explain how it will be useful to the poor. This has shaped a mainstream assumption that what the poor do with their lives is only fighting poverty, curing their maladies, escaping death or valiantly educating themselves beneath a streetlight. 
 In reality, most of the time they are just trying to have a good time, like us. And every time a technology has triumphed among the poor, it has been for the same reason that it became popular among the rich: it is fun. 
 Entertainment is not the byproduct of progress; rather, progress is a byproduct of entertainment. The internet, too, arrived in India as something dreadfully important. I used to be sick of all the moral messages that suggested the internet would help the farmer farm better. But the internet became popular because they could watch prank videos. Of course, the internet can save lives, but its life-saving qualities emerge from its prevalence, and that comes only from its frivolity. 
 So, what do I want Musk to say when he curses India for denying him business? “Please let Starlink in; a tribal on a remote atoll in the Andamans can finally watch porn”? This would be honest, and only as ineffective as a billionaire’s phoney concerns about poverty. 
 The perception of the elite that frivolity is a form of luxury, and that the poor are or should be preoccupied with dreary things is one of our worst misdiagnoses of the human condition. 
 This has led to many useless approaches to taking technology to the poor and to fighting poverty itself. For decades, social workers, if you remember the term, tried to take computers to the poor, always using them to educate and reform. They imagined that ending something as grave as poverty needed a solution that had the same gravitas. It never worked. 
 Over a decade ago, when Mark Zuckerberg wanted to woo India with free internet, he thought he must restrict it to a limited set of sites that were ‘useful,’ educating the poor about some stuff and of course it included something about that sacred thing—crops. He excluded high-bandwidth services such as videos. 
 It was a colossal failure, and not because some paranoid activists were brainwashed to believe a restricted internet was against the spirit of the internet. Zuckerberg’s Free Basics failed because it was boring. 
 The idea that the poor must be treated as poor is at the heart of our failure to save them. It is, in fact , one of the most destructive mindsets of all Indian governments. It sets the bar low, and bases policies on the idea that the poor must access only things appropriate to their bad luck. 
 In reality, fun is a basic human need, and hence should be a basic human right. Among the sights that should break your heart, if your heart is as fragile as you say, is of a little girl who lives on the pavement storing half a lipstick as though it is an artefact or staring at the frolic of girls her age, or flouncing her hair while looking into the rearview mirror of a bike. The poor are a lot like rich people but with no means. 
 The root of most of our problems is that people who are lucky enough to be in a position to solve them for other people have to perform a task whose difficulty is underestimated—they have to guess an experience they have never endured themselves. Most people are not good at this. 
 In treating the poor as different people, do-gooders themselves unknowingly behave like feudal lords. For example, there is the insistence that when the poor kill themselves, it can only be for an economic reason. There is an unspoken view that it is appropriate only for the rich to have mental health issues. As a result, even as physical health care for the poor has vastly improved in India, mental health care is still treated as a luxury, like air-conditioning. 
 When Zuckerberg offered his doomed free internet for the poor, many activists fought it on an obscure theological principle called ‘net neutrality,’ the idea that the internet should be the same for everyone. 
 In compensation, some of them suggested that the poor be given some data free every month, but then others objected that it would be squandered by the poor who would watch porn, just as people fear beggars would squander your loose change on “a film.” Because only the rich should be able to do these things. The poor are supposed to do serious stuff as though they are actors in a Satyajit Ray film. 
 The activists influenced India to ban Free Basics. Most of India’s poor hadn’t experienced the internet then. Months later, Mukesh Ambani’s

 Mint Explainer: What’s at stake for consumer companies this festive season?
 Soumya Gupta 3 min read 18 Oct 2026, 03:33 PM IST 
 Summary
 A split calendar across Q2 and Q3, coupled with rising input costs and inflation, is forcing consumer firms to absorb expenses and bet on premium demand during their biggest annual sales window. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 This year’s festive season is split between the second and third quarters, forcing consumer companies to recalibrate their operational plans and earnings projections. 
 At the same time, a steep rise in input costs across industries is squeezing margins during a critical sales window, while persistent inflation threatens to deepen a K-shaped recovery by pushing middle-class households to curtail discretionary spending. 
 So, how crucial is this festive period to India’s consumer economy, and how are companies navigating these headwinds to drive growth? Mint explains. 
 How important is the festive season for Indian consumer companies?
 Sales during this period are vital, though the impact varies across product categories. Manufacturers of consumer staples such as packaged food, sweets, snacks and edible oil typically see a temporary sales spike. However, for businesses selling jewellery, consumer durables, and apparel, the festive period can drive anywhere from a third to more than half of their total annual revenue. Both online and offline channels feature exclusive product launches and steep discounts around Dussehra, Diwali, and other major festivals. Across several categories, particularly fashion, this sales momentum stretches into Christmas and the year-end. 
 What unique challenges are companies facing this festive season?
 Multiple headwinds are reshaping demand projections this year. First, the calendar timing of major festivals has split the core festive period across the September and December quarters. Several consumer firms note this has shifted anticipated sales into October, weakening second-quarter results while potentially lifting third-quarter performance. 
 Second, persistent input-cost inflation is squeezing corporate profitability. Sharp price hikes in crude oil, crude-linked materials like plastic packaging, agricultural inputs like milk and sugar, and key hardware components such as copper and memory chips are putting margins under pressure. In response, most consumer companies have raised prices while offering more conservative discounts this season.
 Are consumers also spending less? 
 Early signals are mixed. While e-commerce platforms report strong initial figures, the festive season remains in motion. However, demand for online-heavy electronics like smartphones and laptops has slowed sharply, as surging memory chip costs forced manufacturers to hike retail prices significantly. Broader inflationary pressures are also weighing on working-class budgets, dampening appetites for mass-market goods. Shares of value apparel chains such as V2 Retail and Vishal Mega Mart slid earlier this month after management teams cautioned that festive consumer spending could remain subdued.
 How are companies fighting to keep festive-season demand alive? 
 To maintain sales momentum, many firms are opting to absorb higher input costs rather than passing them entirely to consumers. For instance, LG Electronics raised prices on air conditioners this month while leaving its broader consumer electronics portfolio untouched. Similarly, despite wholesale milk prices climbing across India over the past two to three months, consumer packaged goods makers like Nestlé have kept retail prices steady while others initially hiked prices earlier this year. Concurrently, retailers are leaning heavily on premium offerings to power top-line growth as rising costs threaten to compress mass-market demand. 
 Is consumption at the risk of being ‘K-shaped’ again? 
 Possibly, though current data does not yet show a pronounced shift. Rising prices for consumer staples and big-ticket discretionary items tend to hit working-class consumers first. Early signs of strain are already emerging in segments like smartphones and value fashion, alongside a slight uptick in bank financing for festive purchases on e-commerce platforms like Amazon. 
 A critical variable is the ongoing El Niño, which threatens upcoming planting and harvest cycles and could depress agricultural incomes. While the government reduced GST rates across several consumer categories last September to stimulate demand and curb persistent K-shaped consumption, those tax benefits have now largely dissipated.

docs.title: Trump's approval is just 33% — but these 3 other poll numbers may worry Republicans more
docs.text: US President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a new low of 33%, with 66% of Americans disapproving of his job performance, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released on October 18. However, three other findings in the survey could pose additional challenges for Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections: widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of living, a lead for Democrats in the race for control of the House, and public opposition to the US military action against Iran.The poll found that Trump's approval rating had declined from 37% in the outlets' April and July surveys. More than half of respondents, or 52%, said they strongly disapproved of his performance.Among likely voters, 38% approved of Trump's performance, while 62% disapproved. The results come just over two weeks before the midterm elections, which will test Republican support and the strength of the party's agenda.1. 71% say gasoline is unaffordable as cost-of-living concerns mountThe first warning sign for Republicans is the extent of public dissatisfaction with household expenses.Around three in four Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living, the survey found. Nearly half of respondents, or 48%, said they were financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025.The findings on gasoline affordability were particularly striking. In February, before Trump launched the war with Iran, 71% of respondents said gasoline was affordable. In the latest survey, the proportion saying gasoline was unaffordable had risen to 71%.The poll's account linked the shift to the war's disruption of supplies and shipping, which pushed up gasoline and diesel prices.Concerns extended beyond fuel. Fewer than four in 10 respondents considered dining out affordable.2. Democrats lead by eight points in the race for House controlThe second potential problem for Republicans is the Democratic advantage in the poll's congressional preferences.Democrats held an eight-point lead over Republicans among registered voters when respondents were asked which party they preferred to control the House of Representatives.The survey also found that 58% of registered voters would choose Democrats, compared with 39% who would choose Republicans, to act as a check on Trump's White House.Democrats were also viewed as more trustworthy on the economy, leading Republicans by 40% to 33%.However, the poll does not establish that Democrats will win control of the House. The results reflect voter preferences at the time of the survey, rather than a prediction of the final election outcome.3. 65% say military action against Iran was a mistakeThe third warning sign concerns Trump's foreign policy, particularly the war with Iran.The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey found that 65% of respondents considered military action against Iran a mistake. Another 68% disapproved of Trump's handling of US allies.Other numbers that could concern RepublicansThe poll highlighted broader concerns about Trump's conduct and the Republican Party's image.- 72% said the country was heading in the wrong direction.- 66% said Trump was using the presidency to enrich himself.- 66% viewed Trump as too extreme.- 55% considered the Republican Party too extreme, compared with 36% who said the same of Democrats.- 63% had an unfavourable view of the Republican Party, compared with 54% who viewed the Democratic Party unfavourably.The survey also found signs of dissatisfaction among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. Among those voters, 23% disapproved of his overall performance, 31% disapproved of his management of the economy and 38% disapproved of his handling of inflation.The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll was conducted from October 9 to 13 among 2,545 US adults. The margin of error was plus or minus two percentage points for all adults and plus or minus 2.2 percentage points for registered and likely voters.

 NIFTY finally saw a week of respite as buyers built on bullish momentum and demand emerged at lower levels. The index advanced nearly 1000 points from its weekly lows, reflecting a significant improvement in buying momentum. The week ultimately concluded on a very encouraging note, with NIFTY closing at 23146, up 2.78 per cent for the week. 
 The sharp 1,000-point rally has helped stage a turnaround in market sentiment and the technical structure, confirming the presence of strong demand at lower levels, particularly in the 23,100–23,200 band. In contrast, broader market indices, particularly the MIDCAP and SMALLCAP indices, remained subdued or ended in negative territory. Going forward, unless the rally witnesses meaningful participation from the broader market, the combination of narrow market leadership and stiff overhead resistance is likely to limit further upside. Under these circumstances, the prevailing risk-reward setup does not particularly favour the bulls at this stage.

IPO review: Jio Platforms' ₹30,213 crore mega offer is at a minor premium
 Brokerages say the firm is well positioned to sustain industry-leading growth, given market leadership, multiple triggers
 premium 
 Jio Platforms is banking on tariff hikes, subscriber upgrades and digital services to strengthen revenue growth and profitability.
 Ram Prasad Sahu Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:15 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Jio Platforms (JPL), the parent of Reliance Jio Infocomm (Jio), is positioning itself as a vertically integrated technology platform, as it seeks to raise up to ₹30,213 crore in the largest initial public offering (IPO) to hit the Indian markets. The pitch to investors goes beyond telephone and data consumption. It is positioning itself more as the next generation digital services and technology platform provider. 
 The company has incurred substantial capital expenditure to build its comprehensive infrastructure and spectrum assets. However, the investment case will be justified only if it reflects on the financials. Given that the company will use the IPO proceeds to pay debt, there should be savings on finance costs, lower leverage and improved profitability. 
 Over financial years 2024-26 (FY24-26), JPL has grown its revenue and operating profit at an annual rate of 15.8 and 17.8 per cent, respectively. While, net profit grew at 18.4 per cent over this period. Piyush Pandey and Heet Shah of Centrum Research believe it is well positioned to sustain industry-leading growth over the medium to long term, on the back of network leadership, large scale infrastructure, and a deepening digital ecosystem. On the revenue and profitability front, there are multiple triggers, such as improved subscriber mix, premium offerings and monetisation of digital services. But the biggest near term boost to financials, in a highly consolidated market with the top three holding over 97 per cent of wireless broadband subscribers, will be tariff hikes. Centrum expects a 12 per cent tariff hike over the next three-four months that will support growth in average revenue per user (ARPU). 
 At the price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 apiece, JPL is valued at 31.7-33.3 times FY26 earnings per share. On the enterprise value to earnings before interest, depreciation, tax and amortisation (Ebitda) metric (EV/Ebitda) the company is valued at 15-15.6 times FY26 financials. 
 Emkay Research says that the issue is reasonably priced compared to growth it has registered. Analysts led by Pranav Kshatriya have a “subscribe” rating to the issue, given its market leadership, pricing power, growth levers and execution record. 
 On one-year forward (FY28) estimates, the stock is valued at 10.5 to 12 times EV/Ebitda and this is at a 12-17 per cent premium to the current implied multiple for Airtel’s India business. Motilal Oswal Research points out that Jio is the market leader in both wireless and home broadband. It has a greater sway on industry’s pricing architecture. However, the brokerage believes that there is no case for a significant discount for Bharti (vs JPL), given Bharti’s superior free cash flow (FCF) generation and higher return on capital employed (RoCE). 
 With easy subscriber gains likely ending, tariff hikes might be the primary driver of earnings growth, Nomura Research said. Investors with a medium to long-term investment perspective can consider the issue, it said. 
 While it is not reflecting fully on the operational and financial metrics, JPL has multiple things going in its favour. Among them are ownership of the backend (its own autonomous network integrated with an artificial intelligence (AI) engine to manage traffic), hardware (set-top boxes, routers, phones), customised operating systems and digital applications (JioTV, JioCloud), which has helped it reduce dependency on third party vendors, gain cost benefits and innovate faster. 
 Among the key monetisation possibilities is international expansion where the company can replicate its success of AI-driven network automation and digital services platforms in overseas markets. Strategic partnerships with local telecom companies and managed service providers will help it expand beyond India, without replicating the entire domestic infrastructure footprint. This is expected to create additional revenue streams. 
 In India, the company, which has 533 million subscribers, 50 per cent share of wireless broadband, and 42.6 per cent share of fixed broadband, seeks to diversify its revenue streams and increase spends per customer by strengthening its presence in enterprise services, cloud computing and the Internet of Things. In home broadband, Jio seeks to expand the market through the fixed wireless access service to remote areas and increase per user revenue in the wired broadband space. 
 The core bread-and-butter proposition continues to remain the expansion of the telecom user base. The company seeks to upgrade users through entry level phones, affordable mobility plans and application (UPI, streaming) usage.

Largecaps are most vulnerable as investors chase mid, smallcaps: Bhansali
 Sushant Bhansali, chief executive officer of Ambit Asset Management discusses where the value is and how he runs a microcap book
 premium 
 Sushant Bhansali, CEO, Ambit Asset Management.
 Shilpa Rangarajan Pravin Palande 7 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:36 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Largecap stocks are the most vulnerable as global investors stay away and domestic investors keep chasing mid and smallcaps amid a market downtrend. According to Sushant Bhansali , chief executive officer of Ambit Asset Management, which manages about ₹3,500 crore, India is likely to attract foreign capital once the artificial intelligence (AI) trade settles. In an interview with Shilpa Rangarajan and Pravin Palande in Mumbai, he discusses where the value is and how he runs a microcap book. Edited excerpts:
 The market has fallen for eight to nine weeks in a row. Why are global investors staying away? 
 Largecaps, I think, are the most vulnerable right now, because they need large doses of capital, and that is provided by global investors. They have no affection towards India at this point, because they are getting good opportunities in other countries. All other markets, including a few emerging markets, are doing quite well. So why should they bet more on India? There is no point in taking a risk on a country like India when US yields are at 5 per cent plus. That's why they are staying away. But I am sure that with every passing week, India is getting more attractive and juicier. At some point, especially when the AI trade nosedives, I think India will look better. 
 It's not that AI will go out of business. But the sensation around it — that revenue will double every quarter — I think that sensation will someday go away, when people realise that it has to happen at a reasonable cost.
 In past global risk-offs, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) sold emerging markets indiscriminately. Why should India benefit this time? 
 Historically, global risk-off episodes have witnessed FPI sell-offs. This time, given the differentiated growth coupled with compelling valuations, we expect a global sell-off led by AI-related businesses might be an opportunity for Indian markets, as we are well positioned as an anti-AI trade.

 Even many bank stocks are trading at their lifetime-low multiples, with decent growth. Credit growth has reached 18-20 per cent. Then, there are a few buckets where earnings have not gone bad, but the long-term outlook, let's say in IT (information technology), has many doubts in people's minds. If that doesn't play out the way people apprehend right now — that everything will go for a toss — then, given what they have been delivering in the last two to three years, there is big money to be made in that sector in the next two to three years.
 Then, I would say consumer discretionary and consumer staples, where most of the companies have not participated, because consumption has been weak post-2022. But whatever the government has done to get it back on track in 2025-26 is already leading to results. So a good Diwali, a good festival season, and a good marriage season in the next six months can change the game for consumer businesses as well. And then, definitely, there are a few which will continue, like capital goods and energy. They have been doing well, apart from the market correction of late. I think that momentum should continue in those sectors for the next couple of years at least.

Those who invested before, know how much they lost, but those who are new, seeing 25 per cent up, I think they are getting very happy. They are getting into either flexi caps, where people are increasingly playing mid and small caps, or into specific mutual fund schemes in the small and midcap space.
 The multiples of small caps are overall just above average, but in many pockets they are very expensive, and in many they are very cheap as well. I think in the last year and a half or so, returns have become very lopsided. Stocks are down 20, 30, 40, 60, 80 per cent from their lifetime highs. There are stocks which are at lifetime highs as well.
 Gains are concentrated in a narrow set of names. How do you separate earnings-led performance from flow-led, and what gives first if systematic investment plan (SIP) flows slow? 
 Given the tough economic environment — with rising inflation, increasing interest rates, and volatile geopolitics — the earnings trajectory is expected to be concentrated, not broad-based, as we have witnessed over the last one year. This bodes well for stock pickers and concentrated portfolios compared to diversified portfolios. Muted flows might be a damper for index returns, but not necessarily for individual stocks as we have seen currently in the largecap segment, which has witnessed massive FPI outflows in the last two years.

docs.title: Apple wants your living room. Everyone else wants the AI engine
docs.text: For twenty-five years, personal computing enjoyed a rare alignment: the laptop built for daily consumer use was also the primary machine for developers and hackers. When Steve Jobs put OS X on a Unix foundation, Apple unified mainstream software design with deep terminal utility. That truce is showing visible cracks. In mid-October, the tech landscape delivered an unmistakable signal: personal computing is splitting into two distinct camps. On one end stands Apple, building seamless, closed appliances for the living room. On the other stand Microsoft, Google, and Meta, engineering open, complex AI runtimes for builders. Tech For Domestic Use: Apple, HomeView, and Ambient Gadgets Apple’s showcase this week put its domestic ambitions front and centre, turning smart homes from passive sensor networks into active command hubs. Between analyst projections around the Apple HomeView smart display and our breakdown on whether the Apple HomeView is useful, the Rs 39,900 device signals a major strategic leap. Powered by Apple's A18 silicon, the 7-inch hub incorporates multi-user facial recognition to surface individual calendars and widgets when recognised family members walk by, while defaulting to a neutral ambient clock and music dashboard for guests. It also functions as a native Thread border router and Matter controller capable of streaming up to nine live camera feeds simultaneously, with an optional Rs 6,900 wall mount. ALSO READAmazon’s Bee wearables use AI to note down important pointers from your gossip Alongside it, the Apple HomePod Mini 2 made its long-awaited debut six years after the original. Repositioned at Rs 18,900 due to persistent global silicon constraints, the S10-powered compact speaker drops casual impulse-buy pricing to target committed ecosystem users. It introduces voice recognition for up to six household members, integrated temperature and humidity monitoring, Sound Recognition for smoke alarms, and modular surround pairing with Apple TV 4K across five colourways. That consumer push is expanding across everyday lifestyle tech: Ambient Wearables: Amazon made a bold pivot into ambient hardware with its Amazon Bee AI wearables. Splitting the concept across two form factors—the $74.99 clip-on Bee Frontier and the $99.99 MagSafe card-sized Bee Eclipse with 21-day battery life—the devices passively record conversations, generating structured summaries and syncing calendar reminders while surfacing contextual shopping prompts. Affordable Audio: Nothing’s sub-brand seized consumer attention with the CMF Speaker M launch, introducing accessible, design-led personal audio tailored for festive shopping. The Handset Dilemma: Ultra-Luxury Foldables vs. Everyday Flagships The divide between practical utility and high-concept tech was most visible in mobile hardware, where folding devices faced intense scrutiny over whether form factors justify extreme price points. Apple’s ultra-premium entry sparked debate over whether its steep Rs 2.99 lakh entry price delivers genuine daily utility: Buyers weighed the iPhone Duo trade-offs against standard Pro Max phones. Despite boasting a 2nm A20 Pro chip, Grade 5 titanium chassis, and dual-screen Apple Pencil Pro support across its 5.4-inch cover and 7.6-inch inner displays, the device trades away Face ID for a power-button Touch ID sensor and omits a telephoto camera. This dynamic crystallised in the iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Fold comparison. While the iPhone Duo sets benchmarks for gapless hinge design and IP68 durability, Samsung’s Rs 1,79,999 Galaxy Z Fold 8 undercuts it by more than a lakh. With an ultra-light 201g chassis, 45W charging, One UI 9 multitasking, and sharper computational zoom, Samsung demonstrated that an eighth-generation device often delivers better everyday ergonomics than a first-generation luxury experiment. Outside foldables, conventional flagships pushed performance envelopes. While Oppo readied ColorOS 17 neural features on its next Find series, OnePlus previewed the upcoming OnePlus 16 flagship, packing a massive 9,000mAh battery, a 185Hz display, and a 200MP camera setup. The Office Room AI While Apple focuses on consumer hardware, its enterprise rivals are taking the opposite route: opening up the software engine to capture developer runtimes. Microsoft used its hardware and Windows on ARM showcase to highlight deep silicon collaboration with NVIDIA. Under the RTX Spark architecture, developers get direct access to local neural processing units and graphics silicon on client machines, sidestepping closed-garden limits. Meta complemented this shift with its release of Meta Muse Spark Open, touting it as an 816-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with a 1-million-token context window designed for coding and autonomous agentic loops. While freely downloadable for independent researchers on Groq and Hugging Face, Meta added a revenue threshold: businesses generating over $20 million annually must sign commercial licensing agreements to deploy API products. ALSO READThings you should consider before buying an iPhone in October 2026 Google is executing a two-pronged strategy of its own: pushing Gemini enterprise workflows to automate back-office operations, while partnering with Unity to embed generative design tools directly into 3D game engines. Physical Pipes: Satellites, Drones, and Rockets The battle extends beyond operating systems into real-world distribution networks: Extreme Mobility: Automotive tech collided with rocketry as details emerged around Tesla's thruster-equipped Roadster. The vehicle integrates SpaceX-derived cold-gas thrusters housed behind the licence plate, promising sub-1-second 0–60 mph acceleration and brief flight capabilities ahead of a targeted 2028 production run. Satellite Broadband: Space tech heated up locally as Starlink's India rollout plans prepare to challenge domestic telecoms like Reliance Jio and Airtel in the race for orbital internet delivery. docs.title: The art theft paradox
docs.text: Imagine stealing a masterpiece worth millions of euros, escaping without being caught, and then discovering that you cannot sell it to anyone without risking arrest. What good is a fortune on canvas if turning it into cash could land you in prison? It is the paradox of the international art-theft trade. Museums are raided, display cases smashed and cultural treasures spirited away in daring operations. Yet the thieves face a problem. The more famous the stolen object, the harder it can be to sell. So why do they keep doing it? And who is willing to buy something that was never theirs to own? France has been confronted with that mystery again. In early October, thieves stole the enormous, jewel-encrusted bronze cover of Salvador Dalí's Livre de l'Apocalypse (Book of Revelation) from the C Karoutzos Contemporary Art Centre in Issoire. The cover, weighing approximately 150 kg, was decorated with gold, precious stones and pearls. The unique book was created between 1958 and 1961 through a collaboration involving seven artists and seven writers. Its owner was devastated, while investigators were left with the question of how such an extraordinary object could disappear. The Dalí theft is not alone. It is part of a wave of robberies that has exposed the vulnerability of cultural institutions across Europe. Thieves struck the Louvre in Paris on October 19 last year, escaping with French crown jewels valued at approximately €88 million. The daytime raid shook confidence in the security of one of the world's most celebrated museums. This year, the museum's Apollo Gallery reopened, but the stolen jewels remained missing. ALSO READThe business of belief In another extraordinary theft in Spain on August 27, burglars raided the Museum of Villena and stole much of its prehistoric Treasure of Villena, a collection of gold artefacts dating back roughly 3,000 years. The raid reportedly lasted less than four minutes. The treasure's gold alone was estimated to be worth at least €1.7 million, although its archaeological and historical significance is far greater than the value of its metal. In Vienna, in August, two men entered the Museum of Applied Arts as ordinary visitors before smashing a display case and stealing a platinum necklace set with 673 diamonds. The necklace had once belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt and was valued at more than £3 million. The brazen daytime robbery illustrated how objects displayed for public enjoyment can become targets for criminals seeking valuable, portable loot. In Sicily, four Renaissance panels by Antonello da Messina were reported stolen from a museum in Messina in August. Meanwhile, a July raid on France's Lalique Museum saw thieves escape with 27 crystal pieces and jewellery valued at approximately €4.5 million. Historic jewels, ancient gold, celebrated paintings and unique works of art are all being targeted. But who buys stolen art? A painting by Renoir or a jewel-encrusted object associated with Dalí may command an extraordinary price in a legitimate market. But once reported stolen, its fame becomes a liability. Auction houses, reputable dealers and collectors face legal and reputational risks if they attempt to trade in it. The answer is that not every stolen artwork is destined for a conventional sale. Some criminals may seek buyers in illicit networks, while others may use stolen objects as collateral, bargaining chips or leverage in negotiations. In some cases, thieves may hope to sell an object for a fraction of its legitimate value to someone willing to ignore its history. Others may target precious materials rather than the artwork itself. For some perpetrators, the challenge of penetrating a museum and escaping with a celebrated object may be part of the attraction. The theft can offer notoriety, a sense of power or the thrill of outsmarting authorities. Political or ideological motives can also drive the destruction, removal or appropriation of culturally significant objects. The two stolen Renoir paintings in France are a good example of the criminal afterlife. Taken from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8, the works were recovered in October, hidden behind a false wall in a private home. Investigators used DNA evidence and vehicle-tracking information to help identify suspects. Prosecutors also said the investigation uncovered suspicions of a possible second museum raid. The paintings had become evidence and objects that had to be concealed. ALSO READThe big coffee break Europol, the European Union's law-enforcement agency, warned in August that museum thefts were becoming more aggressive, with criminals targeting precious metals, gemstones and culturally significant objects. Its findings suggest that the problem extends beyond individual security failures to a wider criminal ecosystem. So, what do art thieves gain? Sometimes money, leverage, sometimes the thrill of the crime. But the rewards are uncertain, and the risks can be considerable.

docs.title: Building crores without perfect plans or best mutual funds: 10 lessons from 3 techies
docs.text: Building a large investment portfolio takes time, discipline and the ability to invest more as your income grows. There is no single formula for becoming a crorepati. Some investors start with small SIPs, while others build wealth by increasing investments as their salaries rise. In this piece, we look at how three professionals from Pune built their wealth through different financial decisions but worked towards a similar goal. Mayuresh Jadav, 35, started investing through a Rs 2,500 monthly SIP and has built financial assets worth around Rs 1.03 crore. Sudhir Dandotiya, 32, has accumulated assets worth around Rs 9 crore, although his net worth is lower after accounting for liabilities. Shubh Patil, 35, has built a portfolio worth around Rs 4 crore and is now thinking about early retirement. Their stories are part of Financial Express Digital's 'Everyday Crorepatis' series, which looks at how ordinary financial decisions, career choices and investment habits shape real-life wealth journeys. ALSO READHe started with 'very bad' mutual funds, yet built Rs 1 crore corpus at 29 Their incomes, family responsibilities and financial circumstances are different. Yet, there are several lessons that other salaried professionals can learn from their experiences. Here are 10 of them. 1. Your first SIP does not have to be big When people think about investing, they often worry that they do not earn enough to start. A monthly investment of Rs 2,000 or Rs 3,000 may seem too small to make a difference. But waiting for a bigger salary can also mean losing valuable time. Mayuresh Jadav started his investing journey with a monthly SIP of Rs 2,500. Over the years, he increased it to around Rs 70,000 as his income improved. Today, he has built financial assets worth around Rs 1.03 crore. His journey shows why the first step matters. You do not need to begin with a large investment. You need to begin with an amount you can afford and then increase it as your financial position improves. 2. Growing your salary can be as important as choosing the right fund Investors often spend hours comparing mutual funds, studying returns and looking for the next outperformer. But they sometimes overlook a more important question: how much money can they invest in the first place? Mayuresh's salary increased significantly over his career. Sudhir Dandotiya also saw his annual salary rise from around Rs 4.5 lakh in 2017 to Rs 52 lakh in 2026. Shubh Patil's annual package grew from Rs 3.9 lakh in 2013 to around Rs 40 lakh. These income increases gave them greater capacity to save and invest. A higher salary does not automatically create wealth. Someone who spends every additional rupee may have little left to invest despite earning well. But when income growth is accompanied by disciplined saving, it can accelerate wealth creation. 3. Do not let every salary hike disappear into lifestyle expenses A salary increase can make life more comfortable. You may want a better home, more holidays, a new car or more expensive hobbies. There is nothing wrong with spending on things you enjoy. The problem begins when every pay hike leads to a similar increase in expenses. All three journeys highlight the importance of controlling lifestyle inflation. Mayuresh increased his SIP as his earnings grew. Sudhir built a large investment portfolio while committing substantial amounts towards mutual fund SIPs and a home loan. Shubh, despite earning around Rs 40 lakh annually, continues to invest around Rs 70,000 a month while spending on travel and hobbies. Their approaches are different, but the underlying lesson is the same. Higher income creates an opportunity to build wealth only when a part of it is saved and invested. ALSO READRs 18,000 to Rs 4.2 lakh a month: How this 26-year-old made Rs 75 lakh in 3 years 4. You do not need to find the best mutual fund to become wealthy Many investors believe that wealth creation depends on identifying the best-performing mutual fund. They keep switching schemes in search of higher returns and worry about missing the next big opportunity. Sudhir's story challenges this thinking. Despite building assets worth around Rs 9 crore, he does not attribute his wealth to exceptional mutual fund selection. His approach has relied heavily on regular investments, rising income and staying invested. Shubh's experience also offers a similar lesson. His wealth has come from several sources, including mutual funds, Indian and US stocks, company shares, retirement savings and other assets. No single investment explains his entire financial journey. This does not mean fund selection is unimportant. Investors still need to consider costs, risk, portfolio overlap and whether a fund suits their goals. 5. Family responsibilities do not have to stop you from investing Personal finance advice often assumes that an investor can put most of their income towards building wealth. Real life is rarely that simple. Mayuresh has supported his parents and contributed towards his sister's wedding. He has also managed loan repayments and household expenses while continuing to invest. His experience is a reminder that people do not always have the luxury of investing without other financial commitments. They may have ageing parents to support, children to educate, medical expenses to meet or family events to fund. The answer is not necessarily to postpone investing until all responsibilities disappear. That day may never come. 6. Do not buy a financial product you do not understand Mayuresh's investing journey was not free of mistakes. One of his biggest was buying an LIC policy on the recommendation of someone he knew without fully understanding the product. He eventually realised it was not suitable for him. After holding it for around eight to nine years, he exited and received only about 70% of the amount he had invested. docs.title: Beyond HAL and BEL: 3 Indian stocks eyeing the $9.4 billion aerospace metals market
docs.text: When we think of the aerospace opportunity in India, the stocks that come to mind are Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL) and Bharat Electronics (BEL). But the fact is that this opportunity set is far broader. It extends from aircrafts to rockets and more. Today, we dive into a relatively niche opportunity that touches companies across the entire spectrum of this industry. The Billion-Dollar Opportunity Hiding Beneath the Wings An aircraft’s weight affects fuel consumption, flight range and payload capacity, making specialised metals essential to aircraft manufacturing. Aluminium alloys help reduce airframe weight, titanium alloys combine strength with lower weight, and nickel-based superalloys withstand the extreme temperatures inside jet engines. As India looks to expand its domestic aerospace manufacturing capabilities, demand for these materials could create opportunities for specialised metal producers. MarketsandMarkets estimates that India’s aerospace materials market will grow from US$324.3 million in 2025 to US$462.8 million by 2030, at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.4%. This estimate covers aerospace materials broadly, rather than specialised metals alone. Global estimates offer a closer look at the metal-specific opportunity. Fortune Business Insights values the aerospace titanium market at US$3.94 billion in 2025, rising to US$4.22 billion in 2026. The broader aerospace special-metals market, which includes titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys and aluminium alloys, was estimated at US$9.4 billion in 2025. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Three listed companies that are tapping into this demand are worth examining - Mishra Dhatu Nigam, PTC Industries and Hindalco Industries, through its subsidiary Hindalco-Almex Aerospace Limited (HAAL). #1 MIDHANI: Making The Alloys Aircraft Engines Rely On Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) is a government-owned manufacturer of specialised metals and alloys for defence, aerospace and other high-performance applications. Its products include titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys and special steels, which serve different requirements in aircraft structures, engine sections and other critical components. The company operates from Hyderabad, with an additional manufacturing facility at Rohtak. Its investment case is based on developing materials that India imports, developing domestic manufacturing capabilities and obtaining approvals from aerospace customers. From Indigenous Forging to International Qualification During 2026, MIDHANI reported successful isothermal forging of a nickel-based superalloy for a fighter-aircraft engine programme using its 6,000-tonne press. Management also disclosed orders covering four grades of superalloys and three grades of titanium alloys for execution during financial year 2026–27 (FY27). The company has not disclosed the value of these specific orders. The company also received GE Aerospace's S400 testing approval, announced on 13 August 2026. Management has described the ability to conduct specified tests locally as a potential service opportunity for customers who might otherwise send samples abroad. MIDHANI's broader quality system lists approvals and assessments involving the Directorate General of Aeronautical Quality Assurance, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Boeing and Airbus, among others. Management has also discussed engagement with GE, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, but customer engagement, audits and qualification are not equivalent to confirmed serial-production contracts. The ₹2,300-Crore Order Book and ₹8,000-Crore Import Opportunity At its August 2026 earnings call, MIDHANI reported an overall order book of approximately ₹2,300 crore and an estimated ₹8,000-crore import-substitution opportunity across titanium alloys, superalloys and special steels. The order book covers the company’s broader business, while the import opportunity represents potential demand, not confirmed orders or assured revenue from aircraft materials. Exports stood at around ₹33 crore, with an open export order book of approximately ₹25 crore at the time of the call. Both figures relate to the overall business. For readers, the key indicators are new aerospace orders, customer approvals and repeat purchases that demonstrate commercial use of its forging and testing capabilities. Quarterly Numbers Reveal The Difference Between Production And Sales MIDHANI reported standalone revenue from operations of ₹239.49 crore in Q1FY27, up 40.46% year on year but down 56.67% quarter on quarter. Standalone profit after tax (PAT) increased 27.4% year on year to ₹16.31 crore, while falling 79.0% sequentially. The company’s reported value of production rose 7.90% year on year to ₹260.36 crore. The difference between production value and revenue is worth monitoring because manufacturing, delivery and revenue recognition may occur at different times. The sharp sequential decline in revenue also illustrates the uneven nature of quarterly sales. Since MIDHANI reports a single business segment, aircraft-specific revenue, margins or profits figures are not available. The Market is Pricing in MIDHANI’s Next Aerospace Chapter Source: Screener.in; Stock Price as on 15th October 2026 MIDHANI shares rose approximately 14% over six months, while the year-to-date return exceeded 22%. The stock has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 58.5. ICICI Securities maintained a Buy rating in its report dated 18 August 2026, with a target price of ₹510 per share. This translated into an implied upside of 21.53% to the brokerage’s target against the closing price of ₹419.65 on 16 October 2026.
