docs.title: The mother-son duo who turned a silver business into a ₹1.75 lakh crore empire
docs.text: Vivek Chaand Sehgal was eighteen when he learned that money could be heavy. Literally. He carried silver bars to the airport in Delhi during the Hunt brothers' boom, feeling the weight of precious metal in his hands and the weight of expectation in his chest. It was 1974. He earned ₹2,500 a month, a small fortune then, enough to make him dream. Twenty-one years later, in 1995, he stood in a factory in Noida and made a decision that would either build an empire or destroy everything. He had just become Chairman of Motherson Sumi Systems. The company made wiring harnesses for cars. Safe business. Steady business. But Sehgal wanted more. He wanted to buy companies that were bleeding, fix them, and make them his own. Everyone said he was crazy. Indian companies didn't buy European manufacturers in those days. They just didn't. He did it anyway. Fifty-four times over the next two decades. The boy who learned to weigh risk in silver Vivek Chaand Sehgal was born in Delhi on 28 September 1956. His father was in the silver business, a well-known jeweller who understood precious metals and the people who traded them. His mother, Swaran Lata Sehgal, was the steady hand in the family, the one who kept things grounded. His grandfather was also a jeweller, so the family knew value. They knew weight. They knew that what glitters isn't always gold, but silver pays the bills too. He went to Birla Public School in Pilani, then got his bachelor's degree from the University of Delhi. Nothing fancy. No IIT, no IIM. Just a middle-class Delhi boy who understood early that business was about relationships and nerve. At eighteen, during the silver boom engineered by the Hunt brothers in America, he was carrying silver to the airport for buyers. He learned to negotiate. He learned to read people. He learned that timing matters more than almost anything else. When to hold. When to sell. When to walk away. ALSO READHe lost his career for telling the truth. Then he built one of India’s most trusted business empires These lessons would matter later. Much later. In 1975, when he was nineteen, his father suggested something. Why not start a business with his mother? The name came easily. Motherson. Mother and son. It signified trust between a mother and her child. They started with silver trading. Simple business. Buy low, sell high, keep your word. But Sehgal wanted to make things. Not just trade them. (Photo: Motherson Sumi Systems) The cable that connected everything By 1977, Motherson had moved from trading to manufacturing. They set up a cable factory in Noida. Electrical wires. The kind that go into everything from fans to cars. It wasn't glamorous. It wasn't sexy. But it was real. They were making something with their hands now, not just moving metal around. The factory was small. The team was smaller. Mother and son, plus a handful of workers who believed in them. They worked long hours. They made mistakes. They learned. Check Out: List of Auto Sector Stocks Then came 1983. And everything changed. Sehgal heard about a new car coming to India. The Maruti 800. The first affordable car that would be assembled locally. He learned that its wiring harness, the nervous system of the car that connects all its electrical components, had been designed by a Japanese company. He saw an opportunity. He didn't write a letter. He didn't wait for an introduction. "I got a visa and I was in Tokyo within ten days!" he recalls in Motherson's official history. Then the door shut. "I pitched for the business, but they refused to show me the factory." So he did what a trader does when the seller won't open the godown. He took samples home, and his small team worked day and night to make the same thing in India. Nobody recorded how many attempts it took, or how many nights. But it worked. When the Maruti plant opened, a handful of Indian-made parts went on display. Motherson's harnesses were among them. The Lifeline of modern mobility: Motherson employees display a complex automotive wiring harness- the "nervous system" that connected the company to global auto giants. (Photo: Motherson Sumi Systems) It was a breakthrough. Not just an order. A statement. An Indian company could make components for a Japanese-designed car. The handshake with Sumitomo In 1983 Motherson made its first automotive part, a harness for Maruti Suzuki. The same year it signed a technical agreement with Tokai Electric, now Sumitomo Wiring Systems. Three years later, in 1986, the two formed a joint venture, Motherson Sumi Systems. This was the real breakthrough. The Japanese brought technology. Motherson brought speed and local know-how. Maruti brought volumes. Customers followed in a steady line. Tata commercial vehicles in 1991. A stock market listing in 1993. Mercedes in 1995. Hyundai and Ford in 1997. Sehgal was managing director until 1995, then became chairman, which he still is. The boy who carried silver was now running a listed company. When one customer was 70 per cent of everything Here's the thing about a breakthrough customer. It can become a trap. In 1997-98 Maruti hit volume problems, and Motherson found that roughly 70 per cent of its business depended on it. The fix was to spread out. A Hyundai harness venture. Then Europe. The first overseas office opened in Graz, Austria, in 1999. In 2002 came the first acquisition, Ireland's Wexford Electronics, and the first overseas plant, in Sharjah. Outlook reported the Irish manufacturing was moved there within 70 days. That fright hardened into a rule the company calls 3CX10. No customer, country or component should exceed 10 per cent of revenue. It sits in every five-year plan, including the one that runs to 2030. So does a 40 per cent ROCE target, in every plan since 2000-05. Motherson has never hit it. Group ROCE was about 18 per cent in FY25. Honestly, it reads less like a forecast and more like a dare. Yet Sehgal insists, "Our best strategy has been not to have a strategy." That was to Autocar Pro

As of today, India’s installed nuclear power capacity stood at around 7.7 gigawatts electric, according to the World Nuclear Association. The government, however, has set a far more ambitious target: 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047. That would require a nearly 13-fold expansion of the existing capacity. The 100 GW Horizon: Sizing India's ₹20 Lakh Crore Nuclear Bet The scale of investment required is equally striking. Estimates from Singapore-based Nuclear Business Platform suggest that achieving this target could require around $214 billion, or approximately ₹20 lakh crore. Private capital and participation will likely play a larger role in supporting the sector's growth. That is where the policy shift becomes important. The SHANTI Act opened the door to private-sector participation in India's nuclear energy industry. The next phase of growth will also depend on technology. Small Modular Reactors are a key part of India's nuclear ambitions, with the Union Budget 2026 allocating ₹20,000 crore towards their development. The government aims to develop and commission five indigenous SMRs by 2033. The broader ambition is to raise nuclear power's contribution to India's electricity mix from around 3% today to 25% by 2050, although achieving that target will depend on execution, financing, technology and regulatory progress. BHEL has an installed base of 179 gigawatts (GW) in conventional utility power, representing a 53% share in India. BHEL’s Nuclear Moat: Dominating India’s Three-Stage Atomic Fleet BHEL accounts for 60% of India's installed nuclear power capacity on the secondary side. It is the only enterprise associated with all three stages of the Indian Nuclear Power Programme. It is the sole domestic supplier of nuclear steam turbines and generators, providing complete EPC solutions for Turbine-Generator islands across 220 MWe, 500 MWe, and 700 MWe ratings. On April 6, 2026, the company achieved a milestone with the first criticality of the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam. It has supplied 15 nuclear utility sets in India totalling 5.4 GW. As India ramps up its clean energy capacity, nuclear power has emerged as a key part of BHEL's non-thermal growth story. BHEL is collaborating with key stakeholders to support the indigenous design and development of Bharat Small Modular Reactors alongside advanced Pressurised Water Reactor (PWR) and PHWR technology platforms. The company has successfully commissioned 3 units of India's highest-rated 700 MWe PHWRs at Kakrapar and Rawatbhata. For these projects, BHEL supplied a wide range of critical systems, including turbine-generator sets, nuclear steam generators, reactor headers, PCP motors, control and instrumentation packages, and generator transformers. The company has developed an in-house advanced condition monitoring system called 'KAMPAN' for 220 MWe nuclear turbines. This system is designed for turbine supervisory instrumentation and vacuum unloader systems. BHEL plans to implement this technology across 7 nuclear units. The company also reported a strong financial performance in Q2FY27. Q2FY27 Financial Performance: Operational Leverage Expands Margins to 11% Revenue grew 24% year-on-year to ₹9,300 crore in Q2FY27. This topline expansion was driven by broad-based execution acceleration across Power and Industrial Segments. docs.title: 3 smallcaps where FIIs sharply raised stakes in Q2 FY27
docs.text: So far in October 2026, Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have already net sold Rs 52,096 crore of Indian equities. This is a continuation of the selling pressure witnessed in the January-March and April-June quarters of 2026. The recent selloff follows a brief reversal in the July-September quarter, when FIIs turned net buyers . The Nifty Smallcap index rose marginally during this quarter, climbing around 2%, but the movement was uneven. In our earlier story of three microcap stocks that saw the biggest increases in FII holdings, we examined stocks where foreign investors were raising their exposure despite volatile market conditions. Extending that analysis to smallcap stocks, we look at three companies that recorded large increases in FII shareholding during the September quarter and examine the business developments that may explain the increased interest. To identify these stocks, we screened companies with a market capitalisation of more than Rs 5,000 crore but less than Rs 20,000 crore, and an increase of at least 2 percentage points in FII holdings during the quarter. Then we zeroed in on three stocks with the largest increase in FII shareholding, based on data available as of October 16, 2026. Let’s dig in. The company deals in power transmission towers ranging from 11 kilovolt (kV) to 1200 kV, railway structures, testing stations, monopoles, and more, along with a wide range of PVC pipes and HDPE pipes under its polymer business segment. FIIs raised their stake by 6.2 percentage points in the July-September quarter, taking the total holding to 10.31% at the end of the quarter. Smallcap World Fund emerged as the top foreign investor during the quarter, buying a 4.83% fresh stake in the company. Cohesion MK Best Ideas Sub-Trust comes next with a 1.31% fresh stake purchase during the quarter. Won Rs 2,102 Crore Orders Across Domestic And Export Markets Skipper Ltd. secured orders worth Rs 1,305 crore in August for the supply of transmission towers and monopoles for projects in North America, along with two 765 kV transmission line projects from a domestic developer. In September, the company won additional orders worth Rs 797 crore, including export orders for transmission towers and monopoles for projects in Australia and a domestic 765 kV transmission line project. The company’s order book already stood at a record Rs 9,217 crore at the end of June 2026, and these new orders further added to the revenue visibility of the company. 4.5 Lakh Tonne Capacity Target Support Expansion Skipper is expanding its installed capacity to 4.5 lakh tonnes with an ongoing 75,000 tonne expansion. The current manufacturing capacity is around 3.75 lakh tonnes annually. The company has also set a longer-term target, which is to achieve 6 lakh tonnes capacity by FY29. Revenue Rises 4.5%, While Net Profit Grows 26.5% To Rs 56.5 Crore The revenue for the April-June quarter increased 4.5% YoY to Rs 1,309.8 crore, while earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 10.2% to Rs 140.1 crore, with the margin expanding to 10.7% from 10.1%. Net profit grew faster than revenue to Rs 56.5 crore in Q1FY27, compared to Rs 44.7 crore a year ago, logging a 26.5% YoY growth. Management expects revenue to grow around 15% YoY for the full fiscal year 2027 and order inflows to exceed Rs 7,000 crore, with stronger execution in the second half. Skipper's 23.52% ROCE Is In Line With Peer Median, But Debt-to-Equity Is Nearly 4 Times Higher Return on capital employed (ROCE) stood at 23.52%, at par with the peer median of 23.51%. However, Skipper's debt-to-equity ratio (D/E) of 0.63x was nearly four times the industry median of 0.16x, which makes debt levels and the company’s ability to improve capital efficiency important factors to track as it expands manufacturing capacity and executes its order book. Is Skipper Still Undervalued? The stock is trading at a price/earnings (P/E) ratio of 28.3x, lower than the industry median of 33.9x. Its Price/earnings to growth (PEG) ratio also stands at 0.32x, significantly lower than the industry median of 0.65x, indicating the stock is relatively cheaper than its peers. 1-Year Share Price Chart of Skipper Ltd. #2 Sedemac Mechatronics: FII Holding Rises To 10.30%, Net Profit Jumps 95% Sedemac Mechatronics Ltd. is involved in the auto ancillary business, offering design and supply of electronic control units (ECUs) for vehicle and industrial original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) in India, and also caters to the US and European markets. The company’s main focus is on control-intensive ECUs which incorporate technologies that are developed in-house. As of July 2026, the company has sold more than 13 million of such ECUs mainly to major vehicle and industrial OEMs. ALSO READSunil Singhania’s latest PSU bet has a bullet train order bigger than its annual sales FIIs raised their stake by 6.03 percentage points in Q2FY27, taking their total holding to 10.30% at the end of the quarter. docs.title: Relief in Delhi, Anger in Kyiv: Zelenskyy hits out at Trump’s Russian oil sanctions waiver
docs.text: US President Donald Trump's recent waiver of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales has offered temporary relief to India's energy security and exporters. However, it has again invited criticism from within the United States and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who warned that the decision will empower Moscow to keep attacking Kyiv. Taking to his official X account, Zelenskyy said that the move to "undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong" to him, and would "definitely" help "only the Russians." As Ukraine launches strikes on Russia in retaliation, Zelenskyy has continued to accuse Moscow of ramping up its attacks on his country. Noting that Russia hit more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday, the Ukrainian president wrote online, "It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people." He further stressed it "certainly does not stop the war." Although the Graham Act was meant to exert increased pressure on Russia, pushing President Vladimir Putin to call off the war in Ukraine, Donald Trump's recent moves have appeared to stray from that path. Having agreed to a separate diesel deal with Moscow, the POTUS recently took aim at Zelenskyy, calling for his replacement. ALSO READUS waiver gives India room to retain cheaper Russian oil The Ukrainian president also noted that Lindsey Graham, who died in July (the law is named after him), had strongly backed US assistance to Ukraine, urging continued bipartisan support to Kyiv. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," wrote Zelenskyy. "It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey … It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest." On the other hand, Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, hailed the Trump waiver as a "truly historic moment" on X, adding that had the sanctions gone into effect, they would have notably impacted economic cooperation between Russia and the US. Russia-related sanctions also targeted India Trump's Friday night executive order waived sanctions and tariffs due next week under the legislation known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, or simply the Graham Act, which was signed into law last month. The law would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on goods from certain importers of Russian oil or gas. India would have been among other countries, including China, owing to its growing imports of Russian oil since the country's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Defending Trump's decision, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Saturday that the US leader now has time to "study" the impact of the sanctions on the global economy. Ahead of his upcoming second official India trip this week, Rubio acknowledged that it was "hard" for New Delhi to move away from Russian energy. "The problem is that these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries, India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," the Trump admin official told reporters. Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) founder Ajay Srivastava, on the other hand, noted that while the waiver "buys time" for India, it doesn't offer any "lasting certainty," as quoted by PTI. "India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed US pressure," he went on. "Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions." India and the US have yet to reach an agreement on a much-stalled bilateral trade pact, with negotiations stretching nearly a year. Just days ago, India's Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said at an event in Delhi that the first tranche of the agreement has been finalised and is "going through final contours, the legal drafting." He emphasised that India seeks to operationalise it once it gets a competitive advantage over peer countries. US divide intensifies after Trump waiver Trump has asserted that the waiver of the Russia-related sanctions and tariffs is in the national interest of the US. He announced the waiver weeks before the November 3 US midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is struggling to maintain its lead in both US Congress chambers while facing intense backlash for fuel price hikes. ALSO READFrance Riots: Historic buildings torched; over 1,000 arrested as student protests escalate A growing share of Americans have panned Trump and his party, with several polls documenting a drop in the POTUS' favourability as more and more citizens, including Republican-aligned Americans, question his handling of the economy amid the ongoing Iran war. Staunch Trump allies are also questioning the POTUS' decision. US Senator Darline Graham, whose late brother the bill is named after, didn't necessarily directly oppose the waiver, but told reporters on Saturday she would have personally chosen to "keep the pressure on Russia" because she didn't trust Putin and his country. Republican Rep. Don Bacon also said that Donald Trump was "prolonging the war, not ending it." GOP Rep. French Hill echoed the sentiment, posting on X that the US should be "increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up." 'Ukrainians sours on US leadership': Survey On the flip side, multinational analytics and advisory company Gallup released a report in late June, revealing results of a survey conducted among Ukrainians in April. It showed a 59-percentage-point drop in US approval among Ukrainians since 2022, marking the largest ever recorded. In comparison, Ukrainian approval of Washington soared from 37% in 2021 to 66% in the early months of the conflict as the United States increasingly provided Kyiv with significant military and financial support. docs.title: Rs 10,500 cr cash, zero debt: Why this high-dividend-yield PSU could pay bigger dividends
docs.text: Welcome to the latest edition of Dividend Hunter. In recent weeks, we have analysed companies where strong cash flows could translate into consistent dividends. In our previous edition, we covered a diversified public sector company that delivered a 3.5% dividend yield This week, in our Dividend Hunter series, we discuss a Navratna central public sector enterprise. The company operates one of India’s largest integrated Bauxite-Alumina-Aluminium-Power complexes. Its revenue and net profit have grown at a 15% and 35% CAGR over the last five years, while the stock price has returned at a 23% CAGR during the same period. For FY26, the company returned 36.3% of its Net Profit to shareholders as dividend distributions, compared to 36.2% in FY25. Significantly, the company's net profit has nearly doubled (by exactly 97%) to ₹5,816.8 crore during the FY22-26 period. Over the same period, dividend per share has increased by 76.9%. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now For FY26, it declared a dividend of ₹2,112.1 crore. This payout included three interim dividends totalling ₹1928.5 crore and a final dividend of ₹183.6 crore. The dividend yield stood at 3.5%. The company is NALCO. NALCO Share Price NALCO Dividend History: How a 97% Profit Jump Boosted FY26 Payouts to ₹11.5/Share NALCO paid a per-share dividend of ₹11.5 in FY26, translating into a dividend yield of 3.5% at the current price (as of October 16) of ₹324. During the year, the company paid three interim dividends totalling ₹10.5 and a final dividend of ₹1.0 per share. The dividend per share has risen 76.9% from ₹6.5 in FY22 to ₹11.5 in FY26, despite a cyclical contraction to ₹4.5 in FY23. Historical Dividend Payout Track Record Financial YearDividend/ShareNet Profit (In Crores)Payout RatioFY22₹6.5₹2,952.040.1%FY23₹4.5₹1,544.555.4%FY24₹5.0₹2,060.044.6%FY25₹10.5₹5,324.736.2%FY26₹11.5₹5,816.836.3%Source: Annual Report, Financialexpress.com Operational Engines: How Alumina and Chemicals Split the ₹17,843 Cr Topline The alumina refinery produces 21 lakh tonnes of alumina hydrate annually. The aluminium smelter has a capacity of 4.6 lakh tonnes per annum. In FY26, the total revenue from operations stood at ₹17,843.05 crore, up 6.3% from the previous year. This revenue is distributed among the aluminium division (72.4%), the chemical division (27.4%) and others (0.2%). Domestic sales rose by 17% to ₹13,027.7 crore, accounting for 73.0% of revenue, driven by strong domestic industrial demand. Meanwhile, export sales declined by 15% to ₹4,701.5 crore, representing the remainder (26.4%) and others (0.6%). In FY26, EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation) rose by 8.7% to ₹8,613 crore, while the margin increased from 47.2% to 48.3%. Consequently, net profit grew by 9.2% to ₹5,816.8 crore. NALCO returned 36.3% of this net profit to shareholders as dividends. ALSO READSunil Singhania’s latest bets: Rs 59 cr into 2 stocks, one below the radar The DIPAM Safety Net: Why a 30% PAT Floor Shields NALCO Shareholders from Dividend Cuts Sustained profitability drives NALCO’s dividend capacity. As per DIPAM guidelines for Central Public Sector Enterprises, NALCO maintains a minimum annual dividend payout of 30% of Profit After Tax (PAT) or 4% of net worth, whichever is higher. Historically, over the past five financial years, NALCO has maintained a payout of more than 35%. Although the payout ratio has declined recently due to strong profit growth, the company’s dividend capacity remains linked to its earnings performance. If NALCO sustains its historical profit growth trajectory, rising earnings could support higher dividend payments in absolute terms, even if the payout ratio remains lower than its historical average. India's per capita aluminium consumption stands at 3.4 kg, compared to the global average of 12 kg, leaving substantial room for domestic market expansion. Demand is driven by government investments in infrastructure, railways, power grids, renewable energy, and electric vehicles. Indian aluminium consumption grew 11.4% in FY26. NALCO is among the lowest-cost producers of bauxite and alumina globally. To capitalise on the demand, the company is expanding its annual alumina refinery capacity from 21 lakh tonnes to 31 lakh tonnes. Production is targeted to begin in October 2026. This could help expand volume. The company is also expanding its operations to source critical minerals. Through a joint venture called 'Khanij Bidesh India Limited' (KABIL), NALCO is securing rights to explore lithium in Argentina to strengthen the domestic battery supply chain. NALCO holds a 40% equity stake in KABIL. This is higher than the ₹5,806.1 crore recorded in FY2025. Operating profit before working capital changes reached ₹7,997.6 crore. After investing ₹2,025 crore in fixed assets, it generated free cash of ₹4,413 crore, down from ₹4,641 crore in FY25. Ganesh Dongre, AVP — Equity Research at Anand Rathi, believes the recovery during the week was supported by buying interest at lower levels, although global uncertainties continue to weigh on overall market sentiment. “Concerns surrounding the US Federal Reserve’s interest-rate outlook, the possibility of further rate hikes by the Fed and the RBI in the coming quarters, and the upward bias in US 10-year Treasury yields remain key factors influencing global risk appetite and foreign institutional investor (FII) flows into emerging markets, including India,” Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said. Factors that may dictate the Indian stock market next week, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, traders should closely monitor Brent crude oil prices, which are approaching their previous highs near $110 per barrel. A sustained move above this level could push crude prices towards $114 per barrel, potentially increasing inflationary concerns and adding pressure on equity markets. So any fresh geopolitical developments, particularly those involving the Middle East and US–Iran relations, could further influence crude oil prices and market sentiment. Therefore, movements in crude oil and developments on the geopolitical front will remain critical factors in determining the market's next directional move. The Anand Rathi expert believes the Nifty witnessed a notable rebound from the 22,000–22,200 support zone and recovered towards the 23,200 mark by the end of the week. This support zone remains crucial, as it represents a significant historical support area near previous yearly and quarterly lows. On the upside, the immediate resistance is placed in the 23,200–23,400 range, followed by the 24,100–24,200 zone, where the 200-day EMA is positioned. “A sustained weekly close above 23,200 would improve the near-term technical outlook and could pave the way for a recovery towards 24,000–24,200. On the downside, the 22,500–22,800 range is expected to act as an important support zone in the coming week, and a decisive break below this range could revive selling pressure,” Dongre added. On the outlook for the Bank Nifty index, the Anand Rathi expert said, the key benchmark index witnessed buying interest during the week, closing at 55,844, up 0.79%. The index is approaching a significant resistance zone around 56,400–56,500, where the 200-day EMA is positioned. “A decisive and sustained breakout above 56,500 would strengthen the near-term technical structure and could open the door for a further recovery. On the downside, 55,000 remains an important support level, and a sustained break below this zone could weaken the recovery and trigger renewed selling pressure,” Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said.
